Subsequently, the Director must prepare and submit the final accounts to the Commission, the Council, the European Parliament, and the Court of Auditors within six months after the end of the financial year. This process culminates in the discharge procedure, where the European Parliament, acting on a recommendation from the Council by a qualified majority, grants the Director formal approval for the budget implementation of the preceding year (year n) before 30 April of year n+2.

In addition to financial reporting, the Joint Undertaking is subject to robust anti-fraud and inspection mechanisms. The European Anti-Fraud Office (OLAF) is granted the same investigative powers regarding the Joint Undertaking and its staff as it holds over Commission departments. Upon the establishment of the Joint Undertaking, it must accede to the Interinstitutional Agreement of 25 May 1999 concerning internal investigations by OLAF, a step that requires approval and necessary facilitating measures from the Governing Board. Furthermore, all decisions and contracts concluded by the Joint Undertaking must explicitly stipulate that both OLAF and the Court of Auditors have the authority to conduct on-the-spot inspections of documents held by all contractors, sub-contractors, and final beneficiaries who have received Community funds, including at the premises of the final beneficiaries.

The financial framework for the Joint Undertaking is structured to align its resource allocation with specific legal agreements and strategic timelines. Resources required to execute tasks defined in Article 1(2)(a) are governed by the ITER Agreement, while those for tasks under Article 1(2)(b) follow the Broader Approach Agreement with Japan. For tasks outlined in Article 1(2)(c), funding is derived from research and training programmes established under Article 7 of the Treaty.

The composition of these resources includes a core contribution from Euratom, inputs from the ITER host State, annual membership fees, voluntary contributions from non-Euratom Members, and additional resources. Based on these parameters, the indicative total resources deemed necessary for the period spanning 2007 to 2041 amount to **EUR 9,653 million**. This total is distributed across two phases: EUR 4,127 million for the initial period (2007–2016) and EUR 1,717 million for the subsequent phase (2017–2041), with a combined constant value total of EUR 5,526 million for the 2007–2011 period.

Within this total, Euratom's indicative contribution is set at **EUR 7,649 million**, with a strict cap of 15% reserved for administrative expenditure. This Euratom allocation is further detailed by programme and period: EUR 3,147 million for 2007–2016, EUR 1,290 million for 2017–2041, and a total of EUR 4,502 million for the 2007–2011 window, of which EUR 2,887 million is attributed to the Seventh Framework Programme (FP7).

By way of derogation from Article 90 of the Treaty, France is authorised to extend the application on the French mainland, to 'traditional' rum produced in its overseas territories, of a rate of excise duty lower than the full rate for alcohol set by Article 3 of Directive 92/84/EEC. This specific provision acknowledges the unique economic and cultural status of these territories, allowing the French mainland to benefit from a reduced tax rate on this specific category of spirit, thereby supporting the preservation of traditional production methods and the distinct identity of rum originating from France's overseas regions.

The derogation specified in Article 1 is strictly limited to rum, as defined under Article 1(4)(a) of Council Regulation (EEC) No 1576/89. To qualify under this provision, the spirit must be produced within the overseas departments using sugar cane that is harvested at the very place of manufacture. Furthermore, the rum must meet specific chemical and physical criteria: it must contain a level of volatile substances (excluding ethyl and methyl alcohol) of at least 225 grams per hectolitre of pure alcohol, and it must possess an alcoholic strength by volume of 40% or higher.

Under the provisions governing excise duties, the reduced rate applicable to the product specified in Article 2 is strictly limited to an annual quota of 108,000 hectolitres of pure alcohol. While this reduced rate is permitted to fall below the minimum excise duty threshold established by Directive 92/84/EEC, it is subject to a lower bound: it cannot be set at more than 50% below the standard national excise duty applicable to alcohol. Consequently, any implementation of this reduced rate must operate within these defined fiscal parameters, ensuring that the discount does not exceed half of the prevailing national standard while remaining within the allocated volume cap.

This Decision is addressed to the French Republic, formally notifying the State of its obligations under the relevant legal framework. It serves as an official instrument to communicate specific directives, rulings, or findings that require the Republic's immediate attention and compliance. By designating the French Republic as the addressee, the document establishes a direct line of accountability, ensuring that the executive and judicial authorities within the nation are aware of the stipulated requirements and the necessary steps to be taken to fulfill them.

**Purpose and Scope**

The primary purpose of this Regulation is to establish the framework under which competent authorities, in compliance with Community law, may intervene in the field of public passenger transport. This intervention is designed to guarantee the provision of services of general interest that market forces alone would fail to deliver adequately. Specifically, the Regulation aims to ensure services that are more numerous, safer, of higher quality, or offered at lower costs. To achieve these objectives, the Regulation sets out the conditions under which authorities may impose or contract for public service obligations. In return for undertaking these obligations, operators may be compensated for their incurred costs and/or granted exclusive rights.

Regarding its geographical and modal application, this Regulation covers the national and international operation of public passenger transport services by rail and other track-based modes, as well as by road. It explicitly excludes services operated primarily for their historical interest or tourist value. Furthermore, Member States have the option to extend the application of this Regulation to public passenger transport by inland waterways and, without prejudice to Council Regulation (EEC) No 3577/92 on maritime cabotage, to national sea waters. However, the Regulation does not apply to public works concessions as defined in Article 1(3)(a) of Directive 2004/17/EC or Article 1(3) of Directive 2004/18/EC.

For the purposes of this Regulation, the following definitions apply to ensure clarity and consistency in the governance of public passenger transport:

**Public passenger transport** refers to passenger transport services of general economic interest provided to the public on a non-discriminatory and continuous basis. The entity responsible for overseeing these services is the **competent authority**, defined as any public authority or group of public authorities of a Member State (or Member States) possessing the power to intervene in public passenger transport within a specific geographical area, or any body vested with such authority. When the geographical scope of such an authority is not national, it is specifically termed a **competent local authority**.

The services themselves are delivered by a **public service operator**, which may be any public or private undertaking, a group of such undertakings, or a public body that operates or provides these services. These operators may be entrusted with specific duties through a **public service obligation**, a requirement defined or determined by a competent authority to ensure services in the general interest that the operator would not assume, or would not assume to the same extent or under the same conditions, without reward. To facilitate this, a competent authority may grant an **exclusive right**, entitling a specific operator to run services on a particular route, network, or area to the exclusion of others.

In exchange for fulfilling these obligations, operators may receive **public service compensation**, defined as any benefit, particularly financial, granted directly or indirectly by a competent authority from public funds during the implementation of a public service obligation. The legal framework for this relationship is established through a **public service contract**, one or more legally binding acts confirming the agreement between the authority and the operator to manage and operate services subject to public service obligations. Depending on national law, this contract may take the form of an individual legislative or regulatory act, or it may contain conditions under which the authority provides services itself or entrusts them to an **internal operator**. An internal operator is a legally distinct entity over which a competent local authority (or a group of authorities including at least one local authority) exercises control similar to that over its own departments.

The awarding of these contracts can occur via a **direct award**, where a contract is given to a specific operator without prior competitive tendering. The financial scope of these arrangements is measured by the **value**, which corresponds to the total remuneration (before VAT) of the operator, including all compensation paid by public authorities and ticket revenue not repaid to the authority. Regulatory measures are generally governed by

Public service contracts and general rules serve as the foundational legal framework for regulating public passenger transport, ensuring that obligations are met with clarity, transparency, and fairness. First and foremost, these instruments must **clearly define the specific public service obligations** the operator must fulfill, along with the precise geographical areas concerned. Furthermore, they must establish, in advance and through an objective and transparent process, the **parameters for calculating any compensation payment** and the **nature and extent of exclusive rights** granted. Crucially, these parameters must be designed to prevent overcompensation; in cases awarded under specific competitive procedures, compensation cannot exceed the net financial effect of the costs incurred and revenues generated, while accounting for revenues retained by the operator and allowing for a reasonable profit. Additionally, the contracts must determine the **arrangements for allocating costs**, which may include staff, energy, infrastructure charges, maintenance of vehicles and rolling stock, fixed costs, and a suitable return on capital, as well as the **allocation of ticket revenue** between the operator and the competent authority.

Regarding the lifespan of these agreements, the duration must be limited, generally not exceeding **10 years for coach and bus services** and **15 years for rail or other track-based modes**. For contracts covering multiple modes where rail represents more than 50% of the value, the limit is 15 years. However, flexibility exists: the duration may be extended by up to **50%** if the operator provides significant assets linked predominantly to the services, or if justified by the particular geographical situation of outermost regions or the amortization of exceptional infrastructure investments awarded through fair tendering. In such cases of extended duration, the competent authority must ensure transparency by transmitting the contract and justifications to the Commission within one year.

Finally, these contracts must address social and operational standards. Competent authorities may require operators to grant **staff rights** equivalent to those in a transfer of undertaking, listing affected employees and their contractual details transparently. Any **quality standards** required by national law must be explicitly included in the tender documents and contracts. Moreover, the extent of **subcontracting** must be indicated transparently; while the primary operator must perform a major part of the services themselves, full subcontracting is permitted for contracts covering design, construction, and operation. All conditions regarding subcontracting must be determined in accordance with applicable national and Community law.

Under the framework governing public service compensation, all financial arrangements linked to a general rule or a public service contract must strictly adhere to the provisions outlined in Article 4, regardless of the specific method used to award the contract. This requirement extends to compensation of any nature associated with contracts awarded directly under Article 5(2), (4), (5), or (6), as well as those stemming from general rules; such payments must additionally satisfy the criteria set forth in the Annex. Furthermore, to ensure regulatory compliance, Member States are obligated to cooperate with the Commission. Upon receiving a written request, they must provide all information deemed necessary by the Commission to assess the compatibility of the granted compensation within a specified timeframe, typically three months, or any longer period explicitly fixed in that request.

Under the regulatory framework governing public service contracts, each competent authority is mandated to ensure transparency and accountability through a structured publication regime. Annually, authorities must release an aggregated report detailing the public service obligations under their jurisdiction, the selected operators, and the specific compensation payments and exclusive rights granted to them as reimbursement. Crucially, this report must distinguish between bus and rail transport to facilitate the effective monitoring and assessment of the network's performance, quality, and financing; it should also clarify the nature and extent of any exclusive rights conferred.

Furthermore, to ensure market openness, authorities must publish specific information in the Official Journal of the European Union at least one year prior to launching an invitation to tender or a direct award. This pre-award notice must include the authority's name and address, the type of award envisaged, and the services and areas potentially covered. However, this requirement is waived if the contract concerns an annual provision of less than 50,000 kilometres of public passenger transport services. Should any published details change, the authority must issue a rectification as soon as possible, though such corrections do not alter the scheduled launch date of the award procedure.

In the specific case of a direct award for rail transport, the authority must disclose additional details within one year of granting the award. This includes the contracting entity's name, ownership structure, and any legal controllers; the contract's duration; a description of the passenger services; the parameters of financial compensation; quality targets regarding punctuality and reliability along with applicable rewards and penalties; and conditions relating to essential assets. Finally, to uphold the principle of reasoned decision-making, if an interested party requests it, the competent authority is obligated to provide the reasons behind its decision to directly award a public service contract.

The Research Programme for the Research Fund for Coal and Steel is hereby formally adopted to serve as a strategic instrument for enhancing the competitiveness of Community sectors linked to the coal and steel industries. This Programme is designed to operate in full alignment with the scientific, technological, and political objectives of the Community, ensuring that its initiatives reinforce rather than duplicate existing efforts. Specifically, it complements the activities undertaken by Member States and integrates seamlessly with the broader Community research landscape, particularly the Framework Programme for research, technological development, and demonstration activities. A core principle of this initiative is the fostering of coordination, complementarity, and synergy between the Research Programme and the Framework Programme, actively encouraging the exchange of information and best practices among projects financed under both schemes. Ultimately, the Research Programme will direct its support toward specific research activities tailored to achieve the distinct objectives outlined for the coal sector in Section 3 and the steel sector in Section 4.

The Research Programme operates fundamentally on a cost-sharing basis through RTD grant agreements, ensuring that the total financial contribution, when combined with any additional public funding, strictly adheres to applicable State aid rules. While public contracts are reserved specifically for the supply of movable or immovable assets, the execution of works, or the provision of services necessary for implementing support and preparatory actions, the maximum total financial contribution as a percentage of eligible costs (as defined in Articles 31 to 35) varies by project type. Specifically, research projects are capped at 60%, pilot and demonstration projects at 50%, whereas accompanying measures, support, and preparatory actions may receive up to 100% of their eligible costs.

Under the terms of the grant agreement, eligible costs are strictly defined to ensure financial transparency and accountability. These costs encompass four primary categories: **(a) equipment costs**, covering the purchase or lease of necessary assets; **(b) staff costs**, including salaries and social security contributions for personnel directly involved in the project; **(c) operating costs**, which relate to the day-to-day expenses required to execute the activities; and **(d) indirect costs**, allocated to cover general overheads not directly attributable to specific project tasks. Crucially, reimbursement is limited exclusively to **actual costs incurred** during the project's execution. Consequently, beneficiaries, associated beneficiaries, and sub-beneficiaries are explicitly prohibited from claiming budgeted estimates or applying commercial market rates; only verified expenditures that have actually been paid out qualify for funding.

The Research and Technological Development (RTD) initiative for the steel industry is strategically designed to revolutionize production methodologies by harmonizing high-volume output with rigorous environmental stewardship. At its core, this program seeks to elevate product quality and productivity through the adoption of eight distinct, cutting-edge techniques that address the entire value chain from raw material to final product.

First, the program targets the foundational stages of production by developing **new and improved iron-ore reduction processes** and advanced **ironmaking operations**, aiming to maximize yield while minimizing the carbon footprint of blast furnaces. Simultaneously, it drives innovation in **electric arc furnace (EAF) processes** to enhance the efficiency of recycling scrap metal, thereby reducing reliance on virgin raw materials. Moving into the core transformation phase, RTD efforts focus on optimizing **steelmaking processes** and refining **secondary metallurgy techniques** to ensure superior chemical purity and mechanical properties in the molten state.

To bridge the gap between liquid steel and solid form, the initiative champions breakthroughs in **continuous casting and near net-shape casting**, including methods that integrate direct rolling to eliminate intermediate steps and reduce energy use. The finishing stages are equally critical, with research dedicated to advancing **rolling, finishing, and coating techniques**, as well as optimizing **hot- and cold-rolling operations** alongside modern **pickling and finishing processes** to achieve precise dimensional tolerances and surface integrity.

Underpinning these physical transformations is a robust framework for **process instrumentation, control, and automation**, ensuring that every stage operates with real-time precision and adaptability. Finally, the program recognizes that sustainability and longevity are inextricably linked, dedicating resources to the **maintenance and reliability of production lines** to minimize downtime and extend asset life. Collectively, these eight areas of focus ensure that the steel industry not only meets current market demands but also leads the way in resource conservation, emission reduction, and energy efficiency.

To ensure the effective implementation of waste recovery strategies, Member States are mandated to enact and enforce the necessary legislative and administrative measures guaranteeing that all waste undergoes recovery operations in strict accordance with the principles outlined in Articles 4 and 13. This obligation serves as the foundational step in transitioning from a linear waste model to a circular economy, prioritizing the reuse, recycling, and energy recovery of materials. Furthermore, to maximize the efficiency and environmental integrity of these recovery processes, the framework explicitly requires that waste be collected separately whenever it is technically feasible, environmentally sound, and economically viable. This separation is critical to prevent contamination; consequently, distinct waste streams must not be mixed with other waste or materials possessing different properties, thereby preserving the quality of recyclable resources and ensuring that recovery operations can proceed without compromising environmental standards or economic viability.

Under the framework governing waste management, Member States are required to implement specific measures regarding waste oils, ensuring these actions do not undermine the existing obligations for hazardous waste management outlined in Articles 18 and 19. Primarily, states must ensure that waste oils are collected separately wherever this is technically feasible. Furthermore, any collected waste oil must be treated in strict accordance with the standards set forth in Articles 4 and 13. To optimize treatment efficiency, Member States should also prevent the mixing of waste oils with other waste types or substances, as well as the blending of waste oils with different characteristics, provided that such separation is both technically feasible and economically viable, since mixing can impede effective treatment.

To facilitate these goals, Member States are empowered to adopt additional national measures tailored to their specific conditions. These may include establishing technical requirements, implementing producer responsibility schemes, utilizing economic instruments, or entering into voluntary agreements to support the separate collection and proper treatment of waste oils. Additionally, if national legislation mandates the regeneration of waste oils, Member States may require that such oils be regenerated if technically feasible. In cases where the transboundary shipment of waste oils is regulated under Articles 11 or 12 of Regulation (EC) No 1013/2006, states may restrict shipments destined for incineration or co-incineration facilities. This restriction is intended to prioritize the regeneration of waste oils within the territory, thereby promoting resource recovery over disposal.

Member States are required to ensure that their competent authorities establish one or more comprehensive waste management plans, developed in strict accordance with Articles 1, 4, 13, and 16 of the relevant Directive. These plans must collectively cover the entire geographical territory of the Member State, leaving no area unaddressed. Each plan serves as a strategic document that begins with a detailed analysis of the current waste management situation within the specific geographical entity. It must outline concrete measures designed to improve the environmentally sound preparation for re-use, recycling, recovery, and disposal of waste, while explicitly evaluating how the plan supports the broader objectives and provisions of the Directive.

To ensure robust planning, the documents must contain specific data points tailored to the geographical level and coverage of the planning area. At a minimum, these plans must detail the type, quantity, and source of waste generated, including projections for waste likely to be shipped across borders, alongside an evaluation of future waste stream developments. They must also inventory existing collection schemes and major disposal or recovery installations, paying special attention to arrangements for waste oils, hazardous waste, and streams governed by specific Community legislation. Furthermore, the plans are required to assess the necessity for new collection schemes, the potential closure of existing installations, the need for additional infrastructure under Article 16, and any associated investments. Sufficient information regarding location criteria for site identification and the capacity of future facilities must also be provided.

Beyond these mandatory elements, waste management plans may include organizational aspects describing the allocation of responsibilities between public and private actors, an evaluation of economic instruments suitable for tackling waste problems while maintaining the smooth functioning of the internal market, details on public awareness campaigns, and measures for the rehabilitation of historical contaminated sites. Finally, all waste management plans must conform to the specific waste planning requirements set out in Article 14 of Directive 94/62/EC and the strategy for reducing biodegradable waste going to landfills as referred to in Article 5 of Directive 1999/31/EC.

Under the framework for the evaluation and review of plans and programmes, Member States are mandated to establish a rigorous cyclical assessment process for their waste management strategies. Specifically, they must ensure that both waste management plans and waste prevention programmes undergo formal evaluation at least once every six years. Following this evaluation, the relevant authorities are required to revise these documents as appropriate to address emerging challenges, technological advancements, or changes in waste generation patterns. Where necessary, these revisions must align with the specific provisions outlined in Articles 9 and 11 of the regulation to maintain legal and operational coherence. Complementing national efforts, the European Environment Agency plays a critical oversight role by being invited to incorporate a comprehensive review of progress into its annual report. This review focuses specifically on the completion status and the effective implementation of waste prevention programmes across the Union, thereby providing a transparent, high-level overview of collective achievements and identifying areas requiring further attention.

Under the regulatory framework outlined in Article 23(1), specific entities—including those defined therein, producers of hazardous waste, and professional collectors, transporters, dealers, or brokers of such waste—are mandated to maintain a rigorous chronological record. These records must meticulously document the quantity, nature, and origin of the waste, alongside relevant details regarding its destination, collection frequency, mode of transport, and the foreseen treatment method. This information must be made available to competent authorities upon request. Regarding the duration of these records, hazardous waste documentation must be preserved for a minimum of three years; however, establishments and undertakings specifically engaged in the transport of hazardous waste are required to retain such records for at least 12 months. Furthermore, documentary evidence confirming that management operations have been successfully executed must be supplied to competent authorities or previous holders when requested. While these requirements are strict for hazardous waste, Member States retain the discretion to extend these obligations to producers of non-hazardous waste.

Under the framework of maritime safety regulations, Member States bear the primary responsibility for establishing a robust system of training and assessment for seafarers. To this end, each Member State must formally designate specific authorities or bodies empowered to execute four critical functions: delivering the training outlined in Article 3; organizing and/or supervising required examinations; issuing certificates of competence as stipulated in Article 11; and granting dispensations provided for in Article 16.

Beyond designation, Member States are obligated to ensure that all training and assessment activities adhere to strict quality and operational standards. First, every training and assessment program must be structured according to written programmes that include necessary methods, media, procedures, and course materials to achieve the prescribed standards of competence. These activities must be conducted, monitored, evaluated, and supported by personnel who are qualified in accordance with specific regulatory criteria.

Crucially, the regulations mandate that in-service training or assessment conducted on board a ship must never adversely affect the vessel's normal operations; personnel may only engage in such activities when they can dedicate their full time and attention to the task. Furthermore, all instructors, supervisors, and assessors must be appropriately qualified for the specific types and levels of training or assessment they conduct, whether on board or ashore.

For in-service training intended to qualify a seafarer for certification, the conductors must possess a deep appreciation of the training programme and specific objectives, be qualified in the relevant task, and, if using simulators, have received appropriate instructional guidance and gained practical operational experience on that specific simulator type. Similarly, supervisors of such training must have a full understanding of the programme and its objectives.

Regarding assessment, any person conducting in-service assessments for certification purposes must demonstrate an appropriate level of knowledge regarding the competence being assessed, be qualified in the specific task, and have received guidance in assessment methods and practice. They must also possess practical assessment experience. If the assessment involves simulators, the assessor must have gained practical experience on that specific simulator type under the supervision and to the satisfaction of an experienced assessor. Finally, when a Member State recognizes a course, institution, or qualification from another entity, it must ensure that the qualifications and experience of the instructors and assessors involved comply with the quality standard provisions of Article 10, incorporating appropriate training in instructional techniques and assessment practices that meet all applicable requirements.

Member States are mandated to ensure comprehensive on-board communication protocols across their flagged vessels to guarantee safety and operational efficiency. For all ships, regardless of type, there must always be effective oral communication channels among the entire crew, specifically designed to ensure the correct and timely reception and understanding of safety-related messages and instructions. On passenger ships, whether flying the flag of a Member State or merely starting and/or finishing a voyage in a Member State port, a specific working language must be established and recorded in the ship's log-book; this language is determined by the company or the master, as appropriate. Every seafarer on these vessels is required to understand this language and, where necessary, give orders, provide instructions, and report back in it. If this working language is not an official language of the Member State, all plans and lists required to be posted on board must include translations into that working language.

Furthermore, on passenger ships, personnel nominated on muster lists to assist passengers during emergencies must be readily identifiable and possess sufficient communication skills tailored to the specific context. These skills should consider a combination of factors, including the languages appropriate to the principal nationalities of passengers on a particular route, the likelihood that elementary English vocabulary can facilitate basic instructions, the potential need for non-verbal communication methods such as demonstrations or hand signals when verbal exchange is impractical, the extent to which safety instructions have been provided in passengers' native languages, and the languages used for emergency broadcasts to convey critical guidance. Specifically for oil tankers, chemical tankers, and liquefied gas tankers, the master, officers, and ratings must be able to communicate with one another in a common working language. Additionally, adequate means must exist for communication between the ship and shore-based authorities, conducted in accordance with Chapter V, Regulation 14, paragraph 4, of SOLAS 74. Finally, when conducting Port State Control inspections under Directive 95/21/EC, Member States must verify that ships flying the flag of a non-Member State also comply with these communication requirements.

To ensure maritime safety and operational competence, Member States are mandated to implement robust frameworks for seafarer training and certification. Specifically, for all seafarers serving on ships covered under Article 2, national authorities must enforce measures guaranteeing that these individuals receive training meeting the minimum standards of the STCW Convention, as detailed in Annex I of this Directive. Furthermore, such seafarers must possess valid certificates as defined in Article 4, or hold appropriate certificates as specified in Article 1(27). In addition to these general requirements, Member States must also ensure that crew members who are required to be certified under Regulation III/10.4 of the SOLAS 74 Convention undergo training and obtain certification strictly in accordance with the provisions of this Directive, thereby aligning national practices with international safety obligations.

To ensure the robust enforcement of the regulatory framework, Member States are mandated to establish comprehensive systems of penalties specifically targeting breaches of national provisions adopted pursuant to Articles 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 through 15, 17, 18, 19, 22, 23, 24, and 29, as well as Annexes I and II. It is not sufficient for these states to merely draft such legislation; they must take all necessary measures to guarantee the effective implementation of these penalty regimes in practice. Crucially, the sanctions prescribed within these systems must adhere to a strict tripartite standard: they must be **effective** in addressing the violation, **proportionate** to the severity of the breach and the circumstances involved, and **dissuasive** enough to deter both the specific offender and the general public from engaging in similar non-compliant behavior in the future.

To ensure the integrity of the maritime certification system, Member States are mandated to implement robust frameworks that prevent fraud and other unlawful practices related to the issuance and endorsement of seafarer certificates. This begins with the obligation to enact and enforce appropriate measures, accompanied by penalties that are effective, proportionate, and dissuasive, thereby creating a strong deterrent against illicit activities. Crucially, each Member State must designate specific national authorities responsible for detecting and combating these irregularities. These designated bodies are required to establish seamless channels for exchanging information with counterparts in other Member States and relevant third countries regarding seafarer certification. Furthermore, Member States must promptly notify the Commission, other Member States, and any third countries with which they have specific undertakings under the STCW Convention of the details of these competent authorities. Finally, to facilitate immediate verification and maintain trust across borders, the competent authorities of any Member State must provide written confirmation or denial of the authenticity of seafarers' certificates, endorsements, or training documents upon the request of a host Member State.

Under the provisions governing Programming and Reporting, the European Institute of Innovation and Technology (EIT) is mandated to establish a robust strategic framework through two primary instruments. First, the EIT shall adopt a rolling triennial work programme, which is formulated based on the Strategic Innovation Agenda (SIA) once it has been officially adopted. This comprehensive work programme must articulate the Institute's major priorities and planned initiatives, accompanied by a detailed estimate of financing needs and their corresponding sources. Upon completion, this document is transmitted to the European Parliament, the Council, the Commission, the European Economic and Social Committee, and the Committee of the Regions strictly for information purposes. Second, to ensure ongoing accountability and transparency, the EIT is required to produce an annual report by 30 June of each year. This report serves as a critical review of the activities conducted during the preceding calendar year, providing an assessment of results against established objectives and timetables. Furthermore, it must analyze the risks associated with carried-out activities, evaluate the efficiency of resource utilization, and offer an overview of the general operation of the EIT.

**19 Budgetary Commitments**

The financial envelope allocated for the implementation of this Regulation over the period from 1 January 2008 to 31 December 2013 is established at EUR 308.7 million. Within this defined financial framework, the annual appropriations required to execute the programme shall be authorised by the budgetary authority, ensuring that all expenditures remain strictly within the pre-agreed limits.

The implementation and control of the European Institute of Innovation and Technology's (EIT) budget are governed by a framework designed to balance regulatory compliance with operational agility. In accordance with Article 185(1) of Regulation (EC, Euratom) No 1605/2002, the EIT adopts its own financial rules, which must generally align with Regulation (EC, Euratom) No 2343/2002. However, recognizing the unique nature of the EIT's mission, these rules may deviate from the standard regulation only when specific operating needs demand it and upon receiving prior consent from the European Commission. This flexibility is crucial to ensure the EIT can effectively pursue its objectives and successfully attract and retain private sector partners.

Operationally, the Director holds the responsibility for executing the EIT's budget. To ensure transparency and accountability, the EIT's accounts are consolidated with those of the European Commission. The process concludes with a formal discharge procedure: upon a recommendation from the Council, the European Parliament is required to grant discharge before 30 April of the year *n* + 2. This discharge covers the Director's implementation of the EIT budget for year *n*, as well as the Governing Board's management of the EIT Foundation.

Knowledge and Innovation Communities (KICs) serve as dynamic hubs designed to foster a European innovation ecosystem through a unique tripartite model. As outlined in their foundational framework, KICs are mandated to undertake specific, high-impact activities: they must drive innovation and investments that possess distinct European added value, seamlessly integrating higher education and research to achieve critical mass and accelerate the dissemination of results. Their research agendas must be cutting-edge and innovation-driven, focusing on areas of key economic and societal interest while leveraging existing European and national research to bolster Europe's global competitiveness. Furthermore, KICs are tasked with advancing education and training at master's and doctoral levels, specifically in disciplines poised to meet future socio-economic needs; this includes cultivating innovation-related skills, enhancing managerial and entrepreneurial capabilities, and promoting the mobility of researchers and students. Crucially, they act as disseminators of best practices, prioritizing the development of robust cooperation between higher education, research institutions, and the business sector, including financial and service industries.

To effectively execute this ambitious mandate, KICs are granted substantial overall autonomy. This independence allows them to define their internal organization, composition, precise agenda, and working methods without undue restriction. This flexibility is complemented by an open-door policy, encouraging KICs to welcome new members whenever their participation adds tangible value to the partnership. Finally, the operational relationship between the European Institute of Innovation and Technology (EIT) and each individual KIC is formalized through a contractual agreement, ensuring a structured yet adaptable framework for collaboration and accountability.

Under the framework of the European Institute of Innovation and Technology (EIT), the awarding of degrees and diplomas is governed by a balance between national sovereignty and the unique, integrated nature of Knowledge and Innovation Communities (KICs). As stipulated in the relevant provisions, degrees and diplomas associated with higher education activities must be conferred by participating institutions in strict adherence to their respective national rules and accreditation procedures. However, the agreement between the EIT and the KICs introduces a distinctive feature: these qualifications may also bear the specific label of "EIT degrees and diplomas," thereby signaling their origin within this pan-European innovation ecosystem.

To further reflect the collaborative spirit of the KICs, the EIT actively encourages participating institutions to award joint or multiple degrees and diplomas, fostering a curriculum that mirrors the integrated approach of the communities. While such joint awards are promoted, the framework remains flexible, allowing for the possibility that a single higher education institution may also award these qualifications. Furthermore, in designing these programs, institutions are urged to align their efforts with broader European strategic goals. This includes taking into account Community actions defined in Articles 149 and 150 of the Treaty, as well as initiatives undertaken within the context of the European Higher Education Area, ensuring that the qualifications produced are not only innovative but also fully compatible with the continent's educational and economic objectives.

Under the framework of the Union Customs Code, Member States are mandated to collaborate closely with the European Commission to establish, sustain, and utilize a unified network of electronic systems. These systems serve as the digital backbone for exchanging information between customs offices and for the centralized registration and upkeep of critical records. Specifically, these registries must encompass data regarding economic operators directly or indirectly involved in customs formalities, as well as detailed records of applications and authorizations related to customs procedures and the status of Authorized Economic Operators. Furthermore, the systems must house information on special decisions granted under Article 20 and facilitate common risk management initiatives as outlined in Article 25. To ensure consistency and security across the Union, the Commission is empowered to adopt measures amending non-essential elements of this Regulation through a specific regulatory procedure with scrutiny. These measures will define the standard forms and content of the data to be registered, establish protocols for the maintenance of such data by Member State customs authorities, and set the precise rules governing access to this information by both economic operators and other competent authorities.

Under the framework of customs legislation, authorities are empowered to enforce strict compliance regarding the introduction of non-Community goods into the customs territory. When obligations concerning these goods are not fulfilled, or when goods are withheld from necessary supervision, the customs authorities must take decisive action. This includes the confiscation, sale, or destruction of the goods to ensure regulatory adherence.

Specifically, goods may be subject to disposal if they cannot be released for several critical reasons: if the declarant fails to allow examination within the prescribed timeframe; if required documentation is unavailable; if import or export duties and necessary guarantees are not paid or secured within the legal period; or if the goods are subject to prohibitions or restrictions. Furthermore, authorities may intervene if goods remain on site unremoved for an unreasonable duration after release, or if it is discovered post-release that the goods no longer meet the conditions for their release. Additionally, goods formally abandoned to the State under Article 127 trigger these disposal measures.

Once non-Community goods have been abandoned, seized, or confiscated, they are automatically deemed to be placed under the temporary storage procedure, providing a structured legal pathway for their subsequent handling, sale, or destruction.

The provisions enumerated in paragraph 1—including the second subparagraph of Article 1(3), the second subparagraph of Article 5(1), the first subparagraph of Article 5(2), Article 10(2), Article 11(3), the second subparagraph of Article 12(2), Article 15(1), Article 16(5), Article 18(4), Article 19(5), Article 20(7), Article 20(8), Article 20(9), the second subparagraph of Article 24(3), Article 25(3), Article 28(3), Article 30(2), Article 31(3), Article 33(5), Article 38, Article 39(3), Article 39(6), Article 43, Article 54, the second subparagraph of Article 55(2), Article 56(9), Article 57(3), the second subparagraph of Article 58, the second subparagraph of Article 59(1), Article 62(3), Article 63(3), Article 65(3), the third subparagraph of Article 67(1), Article 71, the first subparagraph of Article 72(3), Article 76, Article 77(3), the second subparagraph of Article 78(1), Article 78(5), Article 85, Article 86(7), the first subparagraph of Article 87(3), the second subparagraph of Article 88(4), Article 89(2), Article 93(2), Article 101(2), Article 103, Article 105(2), the first subparagraph of Article 106(4), Article 107(3), the second subparagraph of Article 108(1), Article 108(4), Article 109(2), Article 109(3), the third subparagraph of Article 110(1), Article 111(3), Article 112(4), Article 113(3), the second subparagraph of Article 114(2), the second subparagraph of Article 115, the first subparagraph of Article 116(2), Article 119(

Under the framework governing intra-Community travel, customs controls or formalities regarding the cabin and hold baggage of passengers on intra-Community flights or sea crossings are strictly limited. Such inspections may only be conducted where specific customs legislation explicitly mandates them. However, this general rule does not impede the execution of essential security and safety checks, nor does it override checks required to enforce prohibitions or restrictions. To address complex travel scenarios, the Commission is empowered to adopt implementing measures that define the specific cases and conditions under which customs controls may be applied. These measures cover situations involving aircraft or maritime services that originate from or are destined for non-Community locations, including flights with stopovers at Community airports, successive legs on a single vessel involving non-Community ports, and the use of pleasure craft or tourist/business aircraft. Furthermore, the regulations specifically address baggage handling for passengers transferring at Community airports between flights originating from or destined for outside the Community, ensuring that customs oversight is applied precisely where the journey crosses external borders, even if the final leg is internal.

The customs territory of the Community is defined as comprising the full territories of its Member States, including their territorial waters, internal waters, and airspace, subject to specific exclusions. This includes the territories of Belgium, Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Denmark (excluding the Faeroe Islands and Greenland), Germany (excluding Heligoland and the territory of Büsingen), Estonia, Ireland, Greece, Spain (excluding Ceuta and Melilla), France (excluding New Caledonia, Mayotte, Saint-Pierre and Miquelon, Wallis and Futuna, French Polynesia, and the French Southern and Antarctic Territories), Italy (excluding Livigno, Campione d'Italia, and specific national waters of Lake Lugano), Cyprus (in accordance with the 2003 Act of Accession), Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Hungary, Malta, the Netherlands (in Europe), Austria, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovenia, Slovakia, Finland, Sweden, and the United Kingdom (including Great Britain, Northern Ireland, the Channel Islands, and the Isle of Man).

Furthermore, certain territories situated outside the direct territory of the Member States are also considered part of the Community's customs territory based on applicable conventions and treaties. Specifically, the territory of Monaco, as defined in the Customs Convention signed in Paris on 18 May 1963, is included. Additionally, the United Kingdom Sovereign Base Areas of Akrotiri and Dhekelia in Cyprus, as defined in the Treaty concerning the Establishment of the Republic of Cyprus signed in Nicosia on 16 August 1960, are likewise deemed part of the customs territory.

When a visa authority determines to refuse a visa application, it is mandated to ensure comprehensive documentation is added to the applicant's file to maintain transparency and facilitate future processing. First, the file must clearly record status information confirming the refusal, explicitly stating whether the decision was made by the refusing authority itself or on behalf of another Member State. This record must also identify the specific authority responsible for the refusal, including its precise location, along with the exact place and date the decision was finalized.

Furthermore, the application file must detail the specific ground(s) for the refusal, drawn from a defined set of criteria. These grounds include instances where the applicant presents a travel document that is false, counterfeit, or forged; fails to justify the purpose and conditions of their intended stay; or cannot provide proof of sufficient means of subsistence for their stay, return, or transit. Other valid grounds encompass situations where the applicant has already stayed for three months within the current six-month period under a uniform or limited territorial validity visa, or where an alert has been issued in the Schengen Information System (SIS) for the purpose of refusing entry. Additionally, refusals may be based on the applicant being considered a threat to public policy, internal security, public health, or international relations, or on the failure to provide proof of adequate and valid travel medical insurance where applicable. The file must also note if the information submitted regarding the justification for the stay was unreliable, if the applicant's intention to leave before the visa expiry could not be ascertained, or if sufficient proof was not provided that the applicant was unable to apply for a visa in advance, thereby justifying a border application.

Each year, the Council determines the maximum allowable fishing effort for every effort group by Member State, utilizing a baseline established through a specific two-stage process. For the initial year of the Regulation's application, this baseline is calculated as the average effort in kilowatt-days (kW-days) recorded during either the 2004–2006 or 2005–2007 period, depending on the preference of the concerned Member State and based on advice from the Scientific, Technical and Economic Committee for Fisheries (STECF). In all subsequent years, the baseline simply equals the maximum allowable fishing effort set for the previous year.

To determine which effort groups require annual adjustments, the Council evaluates cod catches taken by vessels within each group using data submitted by Member States in accordance with Council Regulation (EC) No 199/2008. A list is then compiled for each area defined in Annex I, aggregating effort groups and their corresponding cod catches (including discards), arranged in ascending order of catch volume. The cumulative catch for each group is calculated by summing its own catch with those of all preceding groups in the list, which is then expressed as a percentage of the total cod catch for that area.

Annual adjustments are triggered for any aggregated effort group where this cumulative catch percentage equals or exceeds 20%. For these groups, the maximum allowable fishing effort is adjusted as follows: if Articles 7 or 8 apply, the baseline is adjusted by the same percentage used for fishing mortality; if Article 9 applies, the baseline is adjusted by the same percentage as the reduction in the Total Allowable Catch (TAC). Conversely, for all other effort groups not subject to these adjustments, the maximum allowable fishing effort remains fixed at the established baseline level.

In situations where the Scientific, Technical and Economic Committee for Fisheries (STECF) is unable to provide advice enabling the Council to establish Total Allowable Catches (TACs) in strict accordance with Articles 7 or 8 due to a lack of sufficiently accurate and representative data, the Council must proceed under a specific precautionary procedure. Under this framework, the decision-making process hinges entirely on the nature of STECF's assessment regarding cod catches. If STECF explicitly advises that cod catches should be reduced to the lowest possible level, the Council is mandated to set the TACs at a level representing a **25% reduction** compared to the TAC established in the previous year. Conversely, in all other scenarios where such an extreme reduction is not advised, the default measure is a **15% reduction** relative to the prior year's TAC. However, this 15% reduction is not absolute; it applies only unless STECF specifically advises that such a reduction is inappropriate given the available information. This mechanism ensures that even in the absence of robust data, a structured and scientifically informed approach to conservation is maintained.

Member States are mandated to establish a robust framework for ship safety and security by ensuring that all designated inspectors strictly adhere to the procedures and guidelines detailed in Annex VI of this Directive. When conducting security checks, these Member States must apply the relevant protocols from Annex VI to all ships falling under Articles 3(1), 3(2), and 3(3) of Regulation (EC) No 725/2004 that call at their ports or anchorages, with the specific exception of vessels flying the flag of the port State of inspection.

Furthermore, the provisions regarding expanded inspections outlined in Article 14 are specifically applicable to roll-on/roll-off (ro-ro) ferries and high-speed passenger craft as defined in Directive 1999/35/EC. In instances where a host State, which is not the ship's flag State, conducts a survey in accordance with Articles 6 and 8 of Directive 1999/35/EC, such surveys must be recorded in the inspection database as either a more detailed or expanded inspection, depending on the scope. These recorded surveys shall be fully integrated into the calculation of inspection commitments for each Member State, provided they cover all items listed in Annex VII, and must be taken into account for the purposes of Articles 10, 11, and 12. While this does not prejudice any operational prevention measures decided under Article 10 of Directive 1999/35/EC, the full suite of measures concerning the rectification of deficiencies, detention, refusal of access, and follow-up actions under this Directive shall apply as appropriate. Finally, to ensure consistency across the Union, the Commission retains the authority to adopt rules for the harmonised implementation of these paragraphs, acting in accordance with the procedure specified in Article 31(2).

**Rectification and Detention Protocols**

When a ship is inspected, the competent authority must first be satisfied that any deficiencies confirmed or revealed are, or will be, rectified in full accordance with the relevant Conventions. However, if the inspection uncovers deficiencies that are clearly hazardous to safety, health, or the environment, the competent authority of the port State where the inspection takes place must ensure the ship is detained or that the specific operation in progress is immediately stopped. This detention order or stoppage cannot be lifted until the hazard is fully removed, or until the authority establishes that the ship can proceed to sea, or the operation resume, without risk to the safety and health of passengers or crew, without endangering other ships, and without posing an unreasonable threat to the marine environment.

In exercising professional judgment regarding detention, the inspector must apply the specific criteria outlined in Annex X. A mandatory ground for detention arises if the inspection reveals the ship lacks a functioning voyage data recorder when such equipment is compulsory under Directive 2002/59/EC. If this deficiency cannot be readily fixed in the port of detention, the authority may either authorize the ship to proceed to the nearest appropriate repair yard for immediate rectification or require the deficiency to be corrected within a maximum period of 30 days, adhering to the guidelines developed by the Paris MOU; in these cases, the procedures of Article 21 apply.

In exceptional circumstances where a ship's overall condition is obviously substandard, the competent authority may suspend the inspection entirely until the responsible parties take necessary steps to ensure compliance with Convention requirements. Should a detention occur, the competent authority must immediately inform the flag State administration in writing, including the inspection report; if this is not possible, notification must go to the Consul or, in their absence, the nearest diplomatic representative of that State. Relevant nominated surveyors or recognized organizations responsible for issuing certificates must also be notified where applicable. These actions do not prejudice additional notification and reporting requirements under the Conventions.

Crucially, when exercising port State control, all possible efforts must be made to avoid unduly detaining or delaying a ship. If a ship is unduly detained or delayed, the owner or operator is entitled to compensation for any loss or damage suffered, and in any instance of alleged undue detention, the burden of proof lies with the owner or operator. To alleviate port congestion, a detained ship may be moved to another part of the port if it is safe to do so, though port congestion itself must never

To ensure maritime safety and environmental protection, Member States are mandated to establish robust reporting protocols involving both pilots and port authorities. Under these regulations, pilots engaged in the berthing, unberthing, or transit of ships within a Member State must immediately notify the competent authority of the port or coastal State whenever their normal duties reveal apparent anomalies that could jeopardize ship safety or threaten the marine environment. Similarly, port authorities are required to instantly inform the relevant port State authority if they identify such anomalies within their jurisdiction.

To facilitate efficient data exchange, Member States must require these entities to report specific details—including ship identification (name, IMO number, call sign, and flag), sailing information (last port of call and destination), and a description of the anomalies—preferably in an electronic format. Crucially, Member States must guarantee that proper follow-up actions are taken on all reported anomalies and that a record of these actions is maintained. Furthermore, the Commission is empowered to adopt implementing measures, such as harmonized electronic formats and standardized procedures, to ensure consistent reporting and response mechanisms across all Member States.

This Directive establishes a comprehensive framework for ship/port interface activities, applying to any vessel and its crew calling at a port or anchorage of a Member State. While France retains the discretion to exclude ports and anchorages located in its overseas departments (as defined in Article 299(2) of the Treaty) from this scope, the Directive explicitly clarifies that inspections conducted by Member States in waters under their jurisdiction, even outside of formal ports, count as valid inspections. Furthermore, these provisions do not diminish the rights of intervention available to Member States under relevant international Conventions. A specific derogation is granted to Member States lacking seaports; if they can verify over a three-year period that less than 5% of vessels calling at their river ports fall under this Directive's scope, they may opt out, provided they communicate the relevant vessel statistics to the Commission upon transposition and report any subsequent changes. Regarding smaller vessels, where a ship's gross tonnage is under 500, Member States must apply applicable Convention requirements and take necessary actions to ensure safety, health, and environmental protection, guided by Annex 1 to the Paris MOU. Additionally, to ensure fair treatment, Member States must guarantee that ships flying the flag of a non-party State are not treated more favorably than those flying the flag of a party State during inspections. Finally, the Directive explicitly excludes fishing vessels, warships, naval auxiliaries, wooden ships of primitive build, government ships used for non-commercial purposes, and pleasure yachts not engaged in trade from its scope.

Under the regulations governing Port State Control, Member States are granted specific flexibility to postpone inspections of Priority I ships when exceptional circumstances arise, ensuring that operational realities do not compromise safety or lead to unjust penalties. A postponement is permissible in two primary scenarios: first, if the inspection can be conducted at the ship's next call within the same Member State, provided no other ports in the Community or Paris MOU region are visited in the interim and the delay does not exceed 15 days; second, if the inspection can be performed at a different port of call within the same region within 15 days, contingent upon prior agreement from the host state. When such a postponement is formally recorded in the inspection database, the missed inspection is not counted against the Member State's compliance metrics. However, this relief is conditional; the ship remains obligated to undergo inspection at its next port of call within the Community.

Furthermore, inspections may be waived without penalty for operational reasons if the competent authority deems the inspection would endanger the safety of inspectors, the vessel, its crew, the port, or the marine environment, or if the ship's call occurs exclusively during nighttime. In cases where ships regularly arrive at night, Member States must implement measures to ensure they are inspected appropriately. Similar exemptions apply to ships at anchorage if they are inspected within 15 days at another location, if the call is too short or occurs at night, or if safety risks preclude the inspection, provided these reasons are documented in the database. Finally, any measures intended to amend non-essential elements of these rules regarding implementation must be adopted through the regulatory procedure with scrutiny outlined in Article 31(3).

The primary purpose of this Directive is twofold: first, to ensure that Member States effectively and consistently discharge their obligations as flag States, and second, to enhance maritime safety and prevent pollution from ships flying the flag of a Member State. It is important to note that this Directive operates without prejudice to existing Community maritime legislation. Specifically, it does not affect the provisions of Article 2(2) of Regulation (EC) No 2099/2002, which establishes the Committee on Safe Seas and the Prevention of Pollution from Ships (COSS), nor does it impact Council Directive 1999/63/EC concerning the Agreement on the organisation of working time of seafarers concluded between the European Community Shipowners' Association (ECSA) and the Federation of Transport Workers' Unions in the European Union (FST).

Under the established committee procedure, the Commission is formally assisted by the Committee on Safe Seas and the Prevention of Pollution from Ships (COSS), which was created pursuant to Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 2099/2002. When specific references are made to this procedural framework, the operational rules outlined in Articles 5 and 7 of Decision 1999/468/EC shall apply, with due regard to the provisions contained in Article 8 of that same Decision. Furthermore, to ensure timely decision-making, the standard period specified in Article 5(6) of Decision 1999/468/EC is explicitly set at two months.

**Scope of Application**

This Directive establishes a clear jurisdictional boundary, stipulating that its provisions shall apply exclusively to the administration of the State whose flag the ship is flying. Consequently, the regulatory authority, enforcement mechanisms, and compliance obligations outlined herein are vested solely in the flag State, rather than the coastal State where the vessel may be operating or the port State where it is docked. This principle of flag State jurisdiction ensures that the legal framework governing the ship's safety, environmental protection, and crew welfare is administered by the nation that has sovereignty over the vessel, thereby maintaining a consistent standard of regulation regardless of the ship's geographic location.

Before a vessel is permitted to operate under the flag of a Member State, that State must first implement appropriate measures to ensure the ship fully complies with all applicable international rules and regulations. A critical component of this process involves rigorously verifying the ship's safety records through all reasonable means available. Furthermore, if necessary, the Member State shall consult with the former flag State to determine whether any outstanding deficiencies or safety issues previously identified remain unresolved. Additionally, whenever another flag State requests information regarding a ship that was formerly under its flag, the Member State granting the new right to fly its flag is obligated to promptly provide details of any outstanding deficiencies and other relevant safety-related information to the requesting State.

By 17 June 2012, every Member State was mandated to establish, put into practice, and sustain a robust quality management system specifically tailored to the operational components of its flag State-related administrative activities. This system was required to be formally certified in strict adherence to applicable international quality standards, ensuring a baseline of reliability and consistency in maritime governance. Furthermore, a rigorous accountability mechanism was introduced for Member States facing regulatory scrutiny: those appearing on the black list, or those listed on the grey list for two consecutive years in the most recent annual report of the Paris Memorandum of Understanding on Port State Control (Paris MOU), were obligated to submit a detailed performance report to the Commission. This submission had to occur no later than four months following the publication of the Paris MOU report. Within this document, the affected Member States were required to conduct a thorough identification and analysis of the primary causes driving their lack of compliance, specifically detailing the factors that led to vessel detentions and the specific deficiencies responsible for their black or grey status, thereby fostering transparency and driving corrective action.

Under the regulatory framework governing UCITS, management and investment companies are mandated to implement a robust risk-management process capable of continuously monitoring and measuring the risk of individual positions as well as their aggregate contribution to the portfolio's overall risk profile. Crucially, these entities must employ a mechanism for the accurate and independent valuation of over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives. Furthermore, they are required to regularly communicate specific details to the competent authorities of their home Member State, including the types of derivative instruments used, the underlying risks, quantitative limits, and the methodologies employed to estimate associated risks for each managed UCITS. To facilitate macro-prudential oversight, competent authorities must ensure that this aggregated information is accessible to both the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) and the European Systemic Risk Board (ESRB) for the purpose of monitoring systemic risks at the Union level.

Regarding the utilization of derivatives, Member States may authorize UCITS to employ techniques and instruments relating to transferable securities and money market instruments, provided these are used for efficient portfolio management and strictly conform to the conditions and limits set forth in the Directive. Such operations must never cause the fund to diverge from its stated investment objectives as defined in its fund rules, instruments of incorporation, or prospectus. A fundamental constraint is that a UCITS's global exposure relating to derivative instruments must not exceed the total net value of its portfolio. This exposure calculation must comprehensively account for the current value of underlying assets, counterparty risk, potential future market movements, and the time available to liquidate positions. While UCITS may invest in financial derivative instruments as part of their investment policy, the exposure to the underlying assets must remain within the aggregate investment limits specified in Article 52, unless specific provisions regarding index-based instruments apply. Additionally, if transferable securities or money market instruments embed a derivative, that derivative component must be factored into compliance with these exposure requirements. Finally, to ensure uniform application, the Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts specifying criteria for assessing risk management adequacy, detailed rules for OTC derivative valuation, and procedures for information communication, while ESMA may develop draft implementing technical standards to support these measures.

Under the regulatory framework governing UCITS, Member States are granted specific flexibility to adjust investment concentration limits while maintaining strict oversight. Without prejudice to the overarching restrictions set forth in Article 56, national authorities may permit Member States to raise the standard limits established in Article 52 by up to 20%. This exception applies specifically when a UCITS fund's investment policy, as defined in its rules or instruments of incorporation, aims to replicate the composition of a recognized stock or debt securities index. For this higher limit to be applicable, three cumulative conditions must be met: the index's composition must be sufficiently diversified, it must serve as an adequate benchmark for the relevant market, and it must be published in an appropriate manner.

Furthermore, in response to unique market dynamics, Member States may authorize an even higher concentration limit of up to 35% under exceptional circumstances. This provision is intended for situations where regulated markets exhibit a high dominance of specific transferable securities or money market instruments. However, this elevated limit is strictly conditional; investments up to this 35% threshold are permitted only for a single issuer, ensuring that the increased risk is not spread across multiple entities but remains contained within a specific, justified context.

To ensure compliance with regulatory standards, all marketing communications directed at investors must be unmistakably labeled as such, maintaining a standard of fairness, clarity, and absolute non-misleading content. Specifically, any communication that functions as an invitation to purchase UCITS units and includes specific details about the fund must strictly avoid making statements that contradict or undermine the significance of the information found in the official prospectus and the Key Investor Information Document (KIID) referenced under Article 78. Furthermore, these communications are required to explicitly inform recipients that a prospectus exists and that the KIID is available for review. Crucially, the message must clearly specify the location and language in which these documents can be accessed, or provide precise instructions on how potential investors may obtain them, ensuring full transparency and accessibility.

Under the framework of this Directive, Member States are granted the authority to derogate from the strict prohibitions outlined in Articles 5 to 8, but only when no other satisfactory solution exists. These exceptions are strictly limited to specific, high-priority scenarios: they may be invoked to safeguard public health and safety, ensure air safety, prevent serious damage to crops, livestock, forests, fisheries, and water resources, or protect flora and fauna. Furthermore, derogations are permitted for essential scientific and educational purposes, including research, teaching, re-population efforts, re-introduction programs, and the breeding necessary to support these activities. Additionally, Member States may allow the capture, keeping, or judicious use of certain bird species in small numbers, provided this occurs under strictly supervised conditions and on a selective basis.

However, the exercise of these derogations is not discretionary in its execution; any authorization must explicitly define the specific species involved, the authorized means, arrangements, or methods for capture or killing, and the precise conditions of risk, time, and place under which they apply. Crucially, the legislation must designate the competent authority empowered to verify that these conditions are met and to decide on the scope, limits, and operators of the measures. To ensure accountability, Member States are required to implement specific control mechanisms and submit an annual report to the Commission detailing the implementation of these paragraphs. Finally, the Commission retains the ongoing responsibility to monitor the consequences of these derogations based on the available information, particularly the annual reports, ensuring that their application remains compatible with the Directive's objectives and taking appropriate corrective steps where necessary.

Under the framework of beef and veal payments, Member States that applied Article 68(2)(a)(i) of Regulation (EC) No 1782/2003, alongside new Member States utilizing the single area payment scheme, are permitted to retain all or a portion of their national ceilings (as defined in Article 40) specifically allocated to the suckler cow premium outlined in Annex VI of that Regulation. When exercising this option, these states must implement an additional annual payment to farmers. This supplementary support is strictly conditioned on the maintenance of suckler cows, adhering to the requirements set forth in Section 11 of Chapter 1 of Title IV of the Regulation, and must remain within the ceiling limits established pursuant to Article 51(2).

Furthermore, for the years 2010 and 2011, a similar mechanism applies to Member States that utilized Article 68(1), Article 68(2)(a)(ii), or Article 68(2)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 1782/2003, as well as new Member States under the single area payment scheme. These entities may retain all or part of their national ceilings corresponding to premiums for the slaughtering of calves, the slaughtering of bovine animals other than calves, or the special male premium. In these instances, an additional payment to farmers is also required. These payments are granted to support the slaughtering of calves, the slaughtering of bovine animals other than calves, and the holding of male bovine animals, subject to the same conditions regarding Section 11 of Chapter 1 of Title IV and the ceiling constraints defined in Article 51(2).

When an application for an individual export authorisation is submitted for dual-use items destined for a location not listed in Annex II, or for any item listed in Annex IV, the applicant must explicitly declare if those items are currently located or will be situated in one or more Member States other than the one where the application was filed. Upon receiving such an application, the competent authorities of the submitting Member State are obligated to immediately consult with the authorities of the affected Member State(s) and share all relevant details. The consulted Member State(s) then have a strict window of 10 working days to communicate any objections; these objections are legally binding on the submitting Member State. If no objections are raised within this period, the consulted states are deemed to have no objection. While exceptional circumstances allow a consulted Member State to request an extension of this deadline, such an extension cannot exceed a total of 30 working days. Furthermore, if a Member State determines that an export might prejudice its essential security interests, it may formally request another Member State to refrain from granting an authorisation, or to annul, suspend, modify, or revoke one that has already been issued. In response to such a request, the targeted Member State must immediately enter into non-binding consultations, which must conclude within 10 working days. Should the requested Member State ultimately decide to proceed with granting the authorisation, it must notify the European Commission and all other Member States via the electronic system specified in Article 13(6).

When an exporter completes the formalities for the export of dual-use items at the customs office responsible for processing the declaration, they must first furnish proof that any necessary export authorisation has been obtained. If the documents provided as proof are not in an official language of the Member State where the export declaration is presented, the customs authorities may require the exporter to submit a translation.
