Under the framework governing the marketing of non-EU Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs) managed by non-EU Alternative Investment Fund Managers (AIFMs) within the European Union, a "passport" is granted to allow such entities to market fund units or shares to professional investors across Member States, provided a strict set of conditions are satisfied.

First, the Member State of reference must ensure that appropriate **cooperation arrangements** exist between its competent authorities and the supervisory authority of the third country where the AIF is established. These arrangements must guarantee an efficient exchange of information necessary for effective supervision. Furthermore, the third country in question **must not be listed** as a Non-Cooperative Country and Territory by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF). Additionally, this third country must have signed agreements with the Member State of reference and all other Member States where the AIF is intended to be marketed. These agreements must fully comply with OECD Model Tax Convention standards and ensure an effective exchange of information regarding tax matters. If there is a disagreement regarding the assessment of these cooperation or FATF status conditions, the matter may be referred to the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) for resolution.

The process is initiated when the non-EU AIFM submits a **notification** to the competent authorities of its Member State of reference. This notification must include specific documentation and information as outlined in Annex III of the Directive. The competent authorities have **20 working days** to review this complete notification. If the AIFM's management complies with the Directive, the authorities must inform the AIFM that it may begin marketing the fund in their territory; otherwise, they may prevent marketing if non-compliance is identified. Upon a positive decision, the AIFM can start marketing immediately from the date of this notification, and the authorities must also inform ESMA.

If the AIFM intends to market the fund in Member States other than its own (host Member States), a separate notification process is required. The AIFM must submit a notification containing the documentation specified in **Annex IV**. The competent authorities of the Member State of reference must then transmit this complete file to the host Member States within **20 working days**, provided the AIFM continues to comply with the Directive. This transmission must include a statement confirming the AIFM's authorization to manage funds with a particular investment strategy. To establish the fibre composition of textile products, specific tolerances must be applied to ensure accuracy while accounting for practical manufacturing realities. First, regarding extraneous fibres, their presence does not need to be declared if they fall below certain thresholds: specifically, less than 2% of the total product weight, provided this amount is technically unavoidable in good manufacturing practice and not added routinely; or less than 5% for products that have undergone a carding process, under the same conditions. Second, a manufacturing tolerance of 3% is permitted between the stated fibre composition on the label and the results of an analysis, calculated separately for each fibre type or the "other fibres" category. This 3% tolerance also applies to the percentage of wool referenced in specific regulatory points. When calculating this tolerance, the total weight considered is that of the finished product minus any extraneous fibres identified under the rules in the first section. Third, these two types of tolerances (for extraneous fibres and manufacturing variance) can be applied cumulatively, but only if the extraneous fibres found are chemically identical to one or more fibres already listed on the label. Finally, for specific products where standard processes require higher variances, the Commission may grant authorisation for elevated tolerances upon a manufacturer's request supported by sufficient evidence of exceptional circumstances; such authorisations are reserved for rare cases and may involve delegated acts to define technical criteria and procedural rules.

The power to adopt delegated acts is vested in the Commission, but this authority is strictly conditioned by the provisions of this Article. Specifically, the Commission is granted the power to adopt such acts for an initial period of three years, commencing on 19 January 2012. To ensure ongoing oversight, the Commission must prepare a report regarding the delegation of power no later than six months before the expiration of this initial three-year term. Following this, the delegation of power shall automatically extend for successive periods of identical duration unless the European Parliament or the Council explicitly opposes such an extension at least three months prior to the end of each period. Furthermore, either the European Parliament or the Council retains the right to revoke this delegation of powers at any time; a revocation decision terminates the specific power delegated therein, taking effect the day after its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union or on a later date specified within the decision, without affecting the validity of any delegated acts already in force. Procedurally, as soon as the Commission adopts a delegated act, it must simultaneously notify both the European Parliament and the Council. Finally, a delegated act adopted under Article 26 shall enter into force only if neither the European Parliament nor the Council has expressed an objection within two months of notification, or if both institutions inform the Commission before that deadline expires that they will not object; notably, this two-month period may be extended by an additional two months at the initiative of either the European Parliament or the Council.

**Article 29: Entry into Force**

This Regulation shall enter into force on the 20th day following its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union. As stipulated, the legal provisions contained herein shall become binding and applicable to all Member States immediately upon the expiration of this twenty-day period, ensuring a uniform transition across the Union without the need for further national ratification procedures.

This Directive establishes a comprehensive common framework of measures designed to promote energy efficiency across the European Union, with the primary objective of ensuring the achievement of the Union's 2020 headline target of a 20% improvement in energy efficiency. Beyond meeting this specific milestone, the legislation aims to pave the way for further enhancements in energy efficiency beyond 2020. To facilitate this progress, the Directive lays down specific rules intended to remove barriers within the energy market and overcome market failures that currently impede efficiency in both the supply and use of energy. A key component of this framework is the provision for the establishment of indicative national energy efficiency targets for 2020, guiding member states toward their collective goals. Importantly, the requirements set forth in this Directive serve as minimum standards; they do not prevent any Member State from maintaining or introducing more stringent measures, provided such measures remain compatible with Union law. Where national legislation provides for these more rigorous standards, the Member State is required to notify such legislation to the Commission.

To promote efficiency in heating and cooling, Member States are mandated to conduct a comprehensive assessment by December 31, 2015, evaluating the potential for high-efficiency cogeneration and efficient district heating and cooling systems. This assessment must incorporate existing national analyses from Directive 2004/8/EC and be updated every five years upon Commission request. Based on these findings, states must adopt policies encouraging local and regional heat markets and perform detailed cost-benefit analyses considering climate, economics, and technical suitability. Where benefits exceed costs, Member States must take measures to develop necessary infrastructure or accommodate cogeneration and waste heat utilization; conversely, they may exempt installations if the analysis reveals no net benefit. Specific cost-benefit analyses are required for new or refurbished thermal installations exceeding 20 MW, waste heat projects, and new district heating networks, with exemptions available for low-operating-hour peak plants, nuclear facilities, and those near geological storage sites. Furthermore, authorization criteria must integrate these assessment outcomes, while guarantees of origin for electricity from high-efficiency cogeneration must be issued under transparent, non-discriminatory rules and mutually recognized across states. Finally, any public support for cogeneration must ensure that electricity originates from high-efficiency sources and that waste heat is effectively utilized to achieve primary energy savings, all in compliance with applicable State aid rules.

Under the framework of this regulation, the European Commission is granted specific powers to adopt delegated acts pursuant to Article 23, ensuring the regulatory regime remains both effective and up-to-date. Firstly, the Commission shall be empowered to review the harmonised efficiency reference values established in the second subparagraph of Article 14(10), allowing for necessary adjustments to maintain high standards of energy performance across the Union. Secondly, to ensure the legislation keeps pace with technological advancements, the Commission shall be empowered to adapt various technical parameters. This includes updating values, calculation methods, default primary energy coefficients, and specific requirements detailed in Annexes I, II, III, IV, V, VII, VIII, IX, X, and XII. These delegated acts enable the regulatory framework to evolve dynamically with technical progress without requiring the full legislative procedure for every minor update.

The power to adopt delegated acts is vested in the European Commission, but this authority is strictly conditioned by the provisions of this Article. Specifically, the Commission is granted the power to adopt such acts for an initial period of five years, commencing on 4 December 2012, pursuant to the mandates outlined in Article 22. However, this delegation is not permanent; either the European Parliament or the Council retains the right to revoke it at any time. A revocation decision terminates the specific power delegated in that decision, taking effect the day after its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union or on a later date specified therein, without affecting the validity of any delegated acts that were already in force at the time.

Regarding the procedural workflow, the Commission must simultaneously notify any adopted delegated act to both the European Parliament and the Council. The act does not automatically become law; rather, it enters into force only if neither institution expresses an objection within a two-month period following notification. This timeline can be extended by an additional two months if either the European Parliament or the Council initiates such an extension. Conversely, if both institutions inform the Commission before the deadline expires that they will not object, the act may proceed to entry into force.

Under the Energy Efficiency Obligation Scheme, each Member State is mandated to establish a framework ensuring that designated energy distributors and retail sales companies achieve cumulative end-use energy savings by December 31, 2020. The core target requires obligated parties to generate new annual savings equivalent to at least 1.5% of the average annual energy sales volume to final customers over the three years preceding January 1, 2013, with transport fuel sales potentially excluded. While Member States may opt for a phased approach or utilize specific exemptions—such as reducing the target to 1% in 2014–2015 or excluding industrial activities listed in Annex I of Directive 2003/87/EC—these adjustments cannot reduce the total required savings by more than 25%.

To fulfill these obligations, Member States must designate obligated parties using objective, non-discriminatory criteria, which may include transport fuel distributors. The required savings must be expressed in either final or primary energy terms using standardized conversion factors. Crucially, the scheme relies on rigorous integrity: savings must be calculated according to specific methods in Annex V, verified through independent measurement, control, and verification systems covering a statistically significant sample of measures, and reported annually to the public.

Beyond the baseline obligation, Member States have flexibility to enhance the scheme's impact. They may incorporate social aims, such as prioritizing measures for households facing energy poverty, or allow obligated parties to count certified savings from third-party energy service providers. The scheme also permits the banking of savings, allowing measures implemented in one year to count toward obligations in adjacent years. Alternatively, Member States may choose not to set up an obligation scheme if they implement other policy measures—such as taxes, financing incentives, regulations, standards, or energy labeling—that demonstrably achieve an equivalent level of savings. Any alternative approach must meet strict criteria regarding transparency, defined responsibilities, independent verification, and the publication of annual trends to ensure no double-counting of savings occurs.

Effective from 1 July 2012, the average wholesale charges that visited network operators may levy on a roaming customer's home provider for regulated data roaming services are subject to a strict safeguard limit of EUR 0.25 per megabyte of data transmitted. This cap is scheduled to decrease progressively, dropping to EUR 0.15 per megabyte on 1 July 2013 and further to EUR 0.05 per megabyte on 1 July 2014. Unless modified under Article 19, this reduced rate of EUR 0.05 per megabyte shall remain in force until 30 June 2022. These average wholesale charges apply universally between any pair of operators and must be calculated over a rolling 12-month period, or any shorter duration remaining prior to the 30 June 2022 deadline. The calculation methodology requires dividing the total wholesale revenue received by either the visited or home network operator for these services by the total number of megabytes actually consumed during the relevant period, with the data aggregated on a per-kilobyte basis for the specific roaming or home network operator involved.

**Transparency and Safeguard Mechanisms for Retail Data Roaming Services**

To ensure fair treatment and financial protection for consumers, roaming providers are mandated to implement robust transparency and safeguard mechanisms throughout the lifecycle of a roaming contract. **Before and after a contract is concluded**, providers must keep customers adequately informed of applicable charges in a manner that clearly explains the financial consequences of data usage, enabling users to monitor and control their expenditure. Crucially, providers must proactively inform customers—both prior to signing and on a regular basis thereafter—of the risks associated with automatic and uncontrolled data connections. Furthermore, providers are required to notify customers, free of charge and in clear language, on exactly how to disable these automatic connections to prevent uncontrolled data consumption.

Upon entering a Member State other than their home country and initiating data services for the first time, customers must receive an **automatic, free-of-charge message** (via SMS, email, or pop-up) detailing their personalized tariff. This message must display the price per megabyte in the currency of the home bill, unless the customer has explicitly opted out. Customers who have opted out retain the right to request this information again at any time without cost.

To prevent bill shock, every roaming provider must offer a **free, opt-in facility** that provides real-time information on accumulated consumption (in volume or currency) and guarantees that spending does not exceed a specified limit without explicit customer consent. Providers must offer default limits that do not exceed **EUR 50** of outstanding charges per monthly billing period (excluding VAT), either as a financial cap or a corresponding volume limit. Customers may also choose higher or lower limits. The system must send timely notifications when usage reaches **80% of the agreed limit**. If a customer fails to respond to a warning that the limit is about to be exceeded, the provider must **immediately cease** providing and charging for regulated data roaming services until the customer explicitly requests to continue. All changes to these limit facilities must be processed within one working day, free of charge, and without affecting other subscription elements.

These protections generally do not apply to machine-to-machine devices. Additionally, providers must take reasonable steps to protect customers from inadvertently incurring charges while in their home Member State, particularly in border regions. Finally, these rules extend to travel outside the European Union, provided the visited network allows real-time monitoring; if real-time monitoring is unavailable abroad, customers must be notified immediately via SMS that consumption tracking and spending guarantees are not active.

**Supervision and Enforcement Framework**

National regulatory authorities serve as the primary guardians of compliance within their respective territories, tasked with the strict monitoring and supervision of roaming providers, particularly those utilizing the mechanisms outlined in Articles 6b, 6c, and 6e(3). To ensure transparency, these authorities must maintain and publicly disseminate up-to-date information regarding the application of key regulatory provisions—including Articles 6a, 6b, 6c, 6e, 7, 9, and 12—making it easily accessible to all interested parties.

In preparation for the review mandated by Article 19, regulators are required to closely track developments in both wholesale and retail charges for voice, data, SMS, and MMS services, with specific attention paid to the outermost regions defined in Article 349 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. Furthermore, authorities must remain vigilant regarding inadvertent roaming in border regions between neighboring Member States, actively monitoring for the use of traffic-steering techniques that could disadvantage customers. They are empowered to collect data on such incidents and implement appropriate corrective measures.

To facilitate effective enforcement, national regulatory authorities possess the power to compel undertakings subject to this Regulation to supply all relevant information promptly, adhering to specified time limits and levels of detail. Beyond reactive measures, these authorities may intervene on their own initiative to ensure compliance. Specifically, where necessary, they may invoke powers under Article 5 of the Access Directive to guarantee adequate access and interconnection, thereby ensuring end-to-end connectivity and interoperability. This is critical in scenarios where customers are unable to exchange regulated roaming SMS messages due to a lack of delivery agreements between networks. Finally, upon identifying any breach of the Regulation's obligations, national regulatory authorities have the authority to demand the immediate cessation of such violations.

In the event of a dispute arising from the obligations set forth in this Regulation between undertakings providing electronic communications networks or services within a Member State, the specific dispute resolution procedures outlined in Articles 20 and 21 of the Framework Directive shall apply. Conversely, should a dispute remain unresolved and involve a consumer or end-user regarding an issue falling within the scope of this Regulation, Member States are required to ensure that the out-of-court dispute resolution mechanisms established in Article 34 of the Universal Service Directive remain available to facilitate a resolution.

As of July 1, 2012, the average wholesale charge that a visited network operator may levy on a customer's roaming provider for regulated roaming calls originating on their network—including origination, transit, and termination costs—shall not exceed **EUR 0.14 per minute**. This cap applies universally between any pair of operators and is calculated as a rolling average over a 12-month period (or the remaining portion of the application period before June 30, 2022).

Following this initial ceiling, the maximum average wholesale charge is scheduled for a phased reduction: it will decrease to **EUR 0.10 per minute** on July 1, 2013, and further drop to **EUR 0.05 per minute** on July 1, 2014. From that point forward, the charge shall remain fixed at EUR 0.05 until June 30, 2022, unless otherwise modified under Article 19.

To determine compliance with these limits, the average wholesale charge is calculated by dividing the total wholesale roaming revenue received by the total number of wholesale roaming minutes actually used for calls within the Union by the relevant operator over the specific period. This calculation is performed on a per-second basis, with an adjustment made to account for the visited network operator's ability to apply an initial minimum charging period of no more than 30 seconds.

An **intragroup transaction** is defined as an Over-the-Counter (OTC) derivative contract entered into between counterparties that are part of the same corporate group, subject to strict regulatory conditions regarding consolidation, risk management, and jurisdiction.

When the counterparty is **non-financial**, the transaction qualifies as intragroup only if both parties are included in the same full consolidation, are subject to appropriate centralized risk evaluation, measurement, and control procedures, and are established within the European Union. If the non-financial counterparty is established in a third country, the European Commission must have adopted a specific implementing act under Article 13(2) regarding that jurisdiction.

For **financial counterparties**, the definition is broader and includes four specific scenarios:
1.  Contracts with another group member where both are fully consolidated, subject to centralized risk controls, and the financial counterparty is either in the EU (or an approved third country) and the other party is a regulated financial entity (such as a financial holding company or institution).
2.  Contracts where both parties belong to the same **institutional protection scheme** (as defined in Directive 2006/48/EC), provided the financial counterparty meets the regulatory requirements of the first scenario.
3.  Contracts between credit institutions affiliated to the same **central body**, or between such an institution and the central body itself.
4.  Contracts with a non-financial group member that meet the same consolidation, risk control, and jurisdictional criteria as the non-financial definition above.

Finally, for these definitions to apply, the counterparties must be considered part of the **same consolidation**. This occurs if they are both included in a consolidation under Directive 83/349/EEC, International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS), or equivalent third-country accounting principles; or if they are covered by the same **consolidated supervision** under relevant EU Directives or equivalent third-country supervision verified by competent authorities.

Under the regulatory framework governing Central Counterparties (CCPs), a robust system of information exchange and oversight is established to ensure stability and compliance. First, CCPs are obligated to proactively notify their competent authorities of any changes in management, supplying all necessary data to verify adherence to governance standards. If a board member's conduct threatens the sound and prudent management of the CCP, the authority is empowered to intervene, including the removal of that individual from the board.

Regarding changes in ownership, any natural or legal person (or group acting in concert) intending to acquire, or further increase, a qualifying holding in a CCP—triggering thresholds of 10%, 20%, 30%, 50%, or resulting in the CCP becoming a subsidiary—must submit a written notification to the competent authority detailing the intended holding size and relevant information. Similarly, proposed vendors must notify the authority of decisions to dispose of holdings or reduce stakes below these critical thresholds. Upon receipt of these notifications and supporting documents, the competent authority must acknowledge them in writing within two working days.

The authority then enters an assessment period, capped at 60 working days from the date of acknowledgement, during which it evaluates the proposed transaction. If further information is required to complete this assessment, the authority may request it in writing by the 50th working day; however, the clock on the assessment period is paused during the time it takes to receive a response, with this interruption limited to a maximum of 20 working days. In cases where the acquirer or vendor is situated outside the Union or not subject to specific EU supervisory directives, this interruption may be extended up to 30 working days.

The outcome of the assessment is decisive: if the authority opposes the acquisition, it must inform the proposed acquirer in writing within two working days of completing the assessment, providing clear reasons for the decision. Conversely, if the authority does not issue an opposition within the assessment period, the acquisition is deemed approved. The authority may also set a maximum timeframe for concluding the transaction, which can be extended if appropriate. Finally, while Member States may make reasons for opposition publicly accessible upon request (or automatically, depending on national law), they are strictly prohibited from imposing notification or approval requirements that are more stringent than those outlined in this Regulation.

Information exchange involving personal data between Internal Market Information (IMI) actors within the European Union and their counterparts in third countries is strictly regulated and permitted only when specific legal conditions are met. First, the data must be processed under a provision of a Union act listed in the Annex, which must be matched by an equivalent legal provision in the third country's domestic law. Second, the exchange must occur in accordance with a valid international agreement that explicitly mandates the application of the relevant Union act by the third country, authorizes the use of the IMI system, and defines the principles and modalities for such data transfer. Third, the third country must guarantee adequate protection of personal data, adhering to the standards of Article 25(2) of Directive 95/46/EC; this includes ensuring that data is used solely for the purpose for which it was originally exchanged, with the European Commission having adopted a formal decision under Article 25(6) of that Directive to confirm this adequacy. In specific instances where the European Commission acts as an IMI actor, the exchange of personal data with third-country counterparts is further governed by Articles 9(1) and (7) of Regulation (EC) No 45/2001. To ensure transparency and compliance, the Commission is required to publish and maintain an up-to-date list in the Official Journal of the European Union detailing all third countries authorized to participate in this information exchange.
This Regulation shall enter into force on the twentieth day following that of its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union.

Financing arrangements under this framework are structured to ensure efficient and targeted support for standardisation activities across the Union. Funding is primarily delivered through two main channels: direct grants or contracts awarded without a public procurement call to European standardisation organisations and national standardisation bodies for core activities defined in Article 15(1), as well as to specific bodies identified by basic acts for collaborative preliminary work. For other eligible bodies and European stakeholder organisations meeting Annex III criteria, financing is granted via competitive calls for proposals or public procurement contracts to support standard development, ancillary tasks, and specific activities outlined in Article 15(1) and Article 16.

The nature of the financial instruments varies by recipient and activity type. European standardisation organisations and qualifying stakeholder organisations may receive either action-specific grants or multi-year operating grants, the latter of which are protected from automatic reduction upon renewal to ensure stability. All financing decisions, including grant amounts and maximum funding percentages by activity type, are determined by the Commission. Furthermore, to guarantee value for money and result-oriented spending, grants for standardisation activities are generally awarded as lump sums. These lump sums are contingent upon the successful adoption or revision of requested European standards within stipulated timelines and the demonstrable inclusion of SMEs, consumer organisations, and environmental and social stakeholders in the standardisation process. Finally, the overarching administrative and financial conditions for these grants are formalised through framework partnership agreements between the Commission and the respective organisations, ensuring alignment with EU financial regulations while maintaining transparency through notification to the European Parliament and Council.

Under the framework of this Regulation, a structured reporting mechanism is established to ensure transparency and accountability within the European standardisation system. First, the European standardisation organisations are mandated to submit an annual report to the Commission, which must provide detailed insights into the application of specific articles (4, 5, 10, 15, and 17), the representation of SMEs, consumer organisations, and environmental and social stakeholders in national bodies, and the extent of ICT usage within the system. Furthermore, these reports must highlight cooperation between national standardisation bodies and European entities. Second, European stakeholder organisations that have received Union financing must also submit annual reports detailing their membership composition and the specific activities carried out under Article 16. Finally, to synthesize this data, the Commission is required to present a comprehensive report to the European Parliament and the Council by 31 December 2015 and every five years thereafter. This periodic report will analyze the annual submissions, evaluate the relevance of financed standardisation activities against Union legislation and policies, and assess potential new measures to simplify financing and reduce administrative burdens for European standardisation organisations.

To ensure clarity and coordination within the European standardisation framework, every European standardisation organisation and national standardisation body is required to publish a comprehensive work programme at least once a year. This document serves as a transparent roadmap, detailing all standards and European standardisation deliverables that the body intends to prepare or amend, those currently under development, and those adopted during the previous cycle, excluding cases where new outputs are merely identical or equivalent transpositions of existing international or European standards.

For each item listed in the work programme, specific details must be provided, including the subject matter, the current stage of development, and any references to international standards used as a basis. Once finalized, these work programmes must be made publicly accessible via the organisation's website or another publicly available platform, with a formal notice of their existence published in relevant national or European standardisation journals. Furthermore, at the time of publication, all bodies must notify other European standardisation organisations, national bodies, and the European Commission; the Commission subsequently disseminates this information to Member States through the committee established under Article 22.

Crucially, this transparency mechanism includes binding obligations to prevent fragmentation. National standardisation bodies cannot object to subjects included in a European work programme nor take actions that might prejudice European-level decisions. Additionally, to safeguard harmonisation, national bodies must refrain from publishing new or revised national standards that conflict with existing harmonised standards. Once a new harmonised standard is published, any conflicting national standards must be withdrawn within a reasonable deadline to ensure a unified regulatory landscape.

European standardisation organisations are mandated to actively encourage and facilitate the appropriate representation and effective participation of all relevant stakeholders in their standardisation activities. This inclusive approach specifically targets small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), consumer organisations, and environmental and social stakeholders. To ensure this participation is meaningful, these organisations must leverage European stakeholder organisations that receive Union financing, engaging them at the policy development level and throughout the entire lifecycle of standardisation work. This engagement spans five critical stages: the proposal and acceptance of new work items; technical discussions on proposals; the submission of comments on draft standards; the revision of existing European standards or deliverables; and the dissemination of information and awareness-building regarding adopted standards. Furthermore, beyond collaboration with market surveillance authorities and research facilities, standardisation bodies must foster technical-level representation for undertakings, research centres, universities, and other legal entities in emerging areas with significant policy or technical innovation implications. Such representation is particularly encouraged when these legal entities have previously participated in Union-funded projects under multiannual framework programmes for research, innovation, and technological development, as established pursuant to Article 182 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union.

To foster a more inclusive and dynamic standardisation ecosystem, national standardisation bodies are mandated to actively encourage and facilitate Small and Medium-sized Enterprises' (SMEs) access to standards and their participation in the standards development process. This commitment is operationalized through several strategic measures: national bodies must identify, within their annual work programmes, those standardisation projects of particular interest to SMEs and ensure these are prioritized. Crucially, access to standardisation activities should be granted without obliging SMEs to become formal members of the national body, thereby lowering entry barriers. Financial accessibility is further enhanced by offering free or specially reduced rates for participation in standardisation activities, providing free access to draft standards, and publishing free abstracts of standards on official websites. Additionally, national bodies may apply special pricing for individual standards or offer bundled packages at reduced costs to maximize value for SMEs.

Beyond domestic implementation, national standardisation bodies are required to exchange best practices with one another, aiming to collectively enhance SME participation and the broader utilization of standards. To ensure transparency and accountability, these bodies must submit annual reports to European standardisation organisations detailing their activities under these provisions, along with all other measures taken to improve conditions for SMEs. Furthermore, to maintain public visibility and allow for scrutiny, these annual reports must be published on the respective national bodies' websites.

The risks enumerated in point 5 of Article 15 encompass a comprehensive spectrum of exposures associated with maritime and aviation operations. Primarily, this includes **physical loss or damage** to seagoing ships, offshore or high-seas installations, and aircraft when such damage arises from perils related to their commercial use; it further extends to goods in transit (excluding passengers' baggage) where the journey involves carriage by these vessels or aircraft. Beyond physical assets, the scope covers **liabilities** incurred from the operation of these ships, installations, or aircraft, provided that for aircraft, the law of the Member State of registration does not prohibit jurisdiction agreements regarding such insurance, as well as liabilities stemming from damage to the aforementioned goods in transit. Additionally, the definition explicitly captures **financial losses** directly connected to these operations, with specific mention of lost freight or charter-hire. The provision also includes any **risk or interest** connected to the items listed in points 1 through 3. Finally, notwithstanding the preceding categories, the definition expressly incorporates all **'large risks'** as defined under Directive 2009/138/EC (Solvency II), ensuring that significant exposures are captured regardless of whether they fit the specific operational descriptions above.

For the purposes of this Regulation, the term **'judgment'** encompasses any decision rendered by a court or tribunal of a Member State, regardless of its specific title, and includes decrees, orders, decisions, writs of execution, as well as rulings on the determination of costs or expenses by a court officer. Specifically regarding Chapter III, this definition extends to provisional or protective measures ordered by a court that has jurisdiction over the substance of the matter; however, such measures are excluded if they were issued without summoning the defendant to appear, unless the judgment containing the measure is served on the defendant prior to enforcement. A **'court settlement'** refers to an agreement either approved by a Member State's court or concluded before one during ongoing proceedings. An **'authentic instrument'** is a document formally drawn up or registered as such in the Member State of origin, where a public or empowered authority has verified both the signature and the content. The **'Member State of origin'** is the jurisdiction where the judgment was given, the settlement was approved or concluded, or the authentic instrument was formally created or registered. Conversely, the **'Member State addressed'** is the Member State where recognition is invoked or where enforcement of the judgment, settlement, or instrument is sought. Finally, the **'court of origin'** denotes the specific court that issued the judgment whose recognition or enforcement is being pursued.

Under the jurisdictional rules governing employment disputes within the European legal framework, an employer domiciled in a Member State can generally be sued in the courts of that same Member State. However, to better protect the employee, the law also permits proceedings to be brought in another Member State under specific conditions. If the employee habitually carries out their work in a particular country, the employer may be sued in the courts of that location, or alternatively, in the courts of the last place where the employee performed their duties. In cases where the employee does not habitually work in any single country—such as in mobile or cross-border roles—the jurisdiction falls to the courts of the place where the business that engaged the employee is situated. Furthermore, these provisions extend to employers not domiciled in a Member State; such an employer may be sued in a Member State's court if the conditions outlined in point (b) of the first paragraph are met, ensuring that the location of the work or the business connection determines jurisdiction regardless of the employer's primary domicile.

Under the jurisdictional framework of the Member States, specific courts are granted **exclusive jurisdiction** regardless of where the parties are domiciled, ensuring that certain legal matters are adjudicated only within the territory most closely connected to the subject matter.

First, regarding **immovable property**, proceedings concerning rights *in rem* or tenancies must generally be heard by the courts of the Member State where the property is situated. However, a notable exception exists for short-term private leases: if a tenancy is concluded for temporary private use not exceeding six consecutive months, and both the landlord and tenant are natural persons domiciled in the same Member State, the courts of the defendant's domicile also possess jurisdiction. Second, disputes involving the **constitution, nullity, or dissolution** of companies, legal persons, or associations, as well as the validity of decisions made by their organs, fall exclusively under the authority of the courts in the Member State where the entity has its **seat**. In determining the location of this seat, the relevant court must apply its own rules of private international law. Third, matters concerning the **validity of entries in public registers** are reserved for the courts of the Member State where that specific register is kept.

Fourth, for **intellectual property rights** such as patents, trade marks, and designs, exclusive jurisdiction lies with the courts of the Member State where the deposit or registration was applied for, took place, or is deemed to have occurred under Union or international instruments. This rule applies whether the issue is raised as a primary action or as a defense, with the specific caveat that the jurisdiction of the European Patent Office under the 1973 Munich Convention remains intact for European patents. Finally, in proceedings related to the **enforcement of judgments**, exclusive jurisdiction belongs to the courts of the Member State in which the judgment is currently being or is intended to be enforced.

Under the framework governing the recognition of judgments within the Member States, the recognition of a foreign judgment may be refused upon the application of an interested party only under specific, strictly defined circumstances. First, recognition will be denied if it is manifestly contrary to the public policy (*ordre public*) of the Member State where recognition is sought. Second, in cases where the judgment was rendered in the defendant's absence, refusal is permitted if the defendant was not served with the initiating documents sufficiently in advance to prepare a defense, unless they failed to challenge the judgment when they had the opportunity to do so. Third, recognition is barred if the judgment conflicts with an earlier judgment between the same parties issued either within the Member State addressed or in another Member State or third State, provided that earlier judgment meets the necessary conditions for recognition in the forum.

Furthermore, specific protections exist for vulnerable parties; if the defendant was a policyholder, insured, beneficiary, injured party, consumer, or employee, recognition may be refused if the court of origin's jurisdiction conflicts with the mandatory rules of Chapter II regarding these categories. Crucially, when examining jurisdictional grounds related to these vulnerable parties, the reviewing court must accept the factual findings upon which the original court based its jurisdiction. The jurisdiction of the court of origin is generally immune from review, and the public policy exception cannot be invoked to challenge rules relating to jurisdiction itself. Finally, any application seeking to refuse recognition must be lodged strictly in accordance with the procedural requirements outlined in Subsection 2 and, where applicable, Section 4.

Under the framework governing countercyclical capital buffers, when a designated authority—or a relevant third-country authority acting in accordance with Article 136(4)—establishes a countercyclical buffer rate exceeding 2.5% of the total risk exposure amount (as calculated per Article 92(3) of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013), other designated authorities are empowered to recognize this higher rate. This recognition allows them to incorporate the elevated buffer into the calculation of institution-specific countercyclical capital buffers for domestically authorized institutions, ensuring a consistent approach to systemic risk mitigation across jurisdictions.

However, this recognition is not automatic; it requires formal transparency. Any designated authority that chooses to recognize a buffer rate above the 2.5% threshold must publicly announce this decision on its official website. This announcement must contain specific, detailed information to ensure clarity and compliance, including: the exact applicable countercyclical buffer rate; the specific Member State or third countries to which the rate applies; the effective date from which institutions in the designated authority's Member State must apply the increased buffer for their internal calculations; and, crucially, if the effective date is set less than 12 months after the announcement, a clear reference to the exceptional circumstances justifying this accelerated timeline. This structured process ensures that while cross-border recognition facilitates regulatory alignment, it is underpinned by rigorous disclosure and adherence to implementation deadlines.

Under the regulatory framework governing capital buffers, Member States are mandated to enforce strict prohibitions on distributions when an institution fails to meet its combined buffer requirement. Specifically, any institution that does not meet this requirement must calculate a **Maximum Distributable Amount (MDA)** in accordance with the prescribed methodology and immediately notify the competent authority of this figure. Crucially, while an institution is in a state of non-compliance, it is strictly prohibited from undertaking specific actions until the MDA has been calculated. These prohibited actions include making distributions connected to Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital, creating new obligations for variable remuneration or discretionary pension benefits, and making payments on Additional Tier 1 instruments.

Once the MDA is established, the institution is further restricted from distributing more than this calculated amount through any of the aforementioned actions. The MDA itself is derived by multiplying a sum of eligible profits—comprising interim and year-end profits not yet included in CET1 capital, net of potential tax liabilities—by a specific factor. This factor is determined by the institution's position within the quartiles of the combined buffer requirement: a factor of 0.0 applies if the institution is in the first or second quartile, 0.4 in the third, and 0.6 in the fourth. The MDA is also reduced by any distributions or payments made in violation of the prohibitions listed earlier.

These restrictions apply exclusively to payments that reduce CET1 capital or profits, provided that a suspension or failure to pay does not trigger an event of default or insolvency proceedings. To ensure transparency and oversight, any institution intending to distribute profits or undertake restricted actions while failing to meet the buffer requirement must notify the competent authority with detailed information, including a breakdown of its capital tiers (CET1, Additional Tier 1, and Tier 2), profit amounts, the calculated MDA, and the specific allocation of intended distributable profits (such as dividends, share buybacks, or variable remuneration). Finally, institutions must maintain robust internal arrangements to ensure the accurate calculation of both distributable profits and the MDA, remaining prepared to demonstrate this accuracy to regulators upon request. For the purposes of these rules, "distributions in connection with CET1 capital" broadly encompass cash dividends, bonus shares, share redemptions, repayments of paid-up capital, and other related capital instrument distributions.

By 31 December 2019, all Member States are required to formally notify the European Commission regarding the implementation and application of the type-approval procedures established under this Regulation. This initial reporting phase serves as a critical data-gathering mechanism to ensure uniform compliance across the Union. Subsequently, utilizing the comprehensive information supplied by the Member States pursuant to paragraph 1, the Commission is mandated to draft and submit a detailed report to both the European Parliament and the Council. This final report, due by 31 December 2020, will provide a thorough assessment of the Regulation's practical application, evaluating its effectiveness and identifying any necessary adjustments to ensure the regulatory framework functions as intended.

By 31 December 2022, the Commission is mandated to submit a comprehensive report to both the European Parliament and the Council concerning the subjects outlined in paragraph 3. This report must be grounded in a thorough consultation of relevant stakeholders and must explicitly take into account existing related European and international standards. The foundational data for this assessment will be drawn from Member States' reports submitted by 31 December 2021, which detail the number of individual approvals granted to vehicles covered by this Regulation prior to their first registration per year by national authorities since 1 January 2016, alongside the specific national criteria used where such approvals deviated from obligatory EU type-approval requirements. Furthermore, this final report shall be accompanied, where appropriate, by legislative proposals and must critically examine the feasibility of including individual approvals within the Regulation based on harmonised requirements.

When applying for whole-vehicle type-approval, manufacturers have the flexibility to select from three primary procedures: **step-by-step**, **single-step**, or **mixed type-approval**. Additionally, manufacturers of specific vehicle categories (notably incomplete vehicles in sub-categories L2e-U, L4e, L5e-B, L6e-BU, and L7e-CU) may opt for a **multi-stage type-approval** process. It is important to note that the **single-step procedure** is the exclusive method applicable to the type-approval of systems, components, or separate technical units.

The **step-by-step procedure** involves the sequential collection of EU type-approval certificates for all constituent systems, components, and units, culminating in the final whole-vehicle type-approval. In contrast, the **single-step procedure** grants approval for the vehicle as a complete unit through one unified operation. The **mixed type-approval** functions similarly to a step-by-step approach but allows one or more system approvals to be finalized during the vehicle's final approval stage without issuing separate EU type-approval certificates for those specific systems.

For **multi-stage type-approval**, one or more approval authorities certify that an incomplete or completed vehicle type satisfies relevant administrative and technical requirements based on its current state of completion. This process requires the vehicle to conform to the particulars in the information folder specified in Article 27 and to meet the technical requirements outlined in the relevant acts listed in Annex II. Crucially, the final stage approval is granted only after verifying that the vehicle meets all applicable technical requirements at that time. This includes a documentary check of all requirements covered by previous approvals granted during the multi-stage process, even if those were issued for a different (sub-)category of vehicle.

Regardless of the chosen procedure, the selection does not alter the substantive requirements the approved vehicle type must comply with at the time of issuing the whole-vehicle type-approval. Furthermore, the Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts to establish detailed arrangements regarding these procedures, with the first such acts required to be adopted by 31 December 2014.

For the purposes of this Regulation and the acts listed in Annex II, except as otherwise provided therein, the following definitions shall apply:

(1) **'Type-approval'** means the procedure whereby an approval authority certifies that a type of vehicle, system, component or separate technical unit satisfies the relevant administrative provisions and technical requirements.

(2) **'Type-approval certificate'** means the document whereby the approval authority officially certifies that a type of vehicle, system, component or separate technical unit is approved.

(3) **'Whole-vehicle type-approval'** means a type-approval whereby an approval authority certifies that an incomplete, complete or completed vehicle type satisfies the relevant administrative provisions and technical requirements.

(4) **'EU type-approval'** means the procedure whereby an approval authority certifies that a type of vehicle, system, component or separate technical unit satisfies the relevant administrative provisions and technical requirements of this Regulation.

(5) **'EU type-approval certificate'** means the certificate based on the template set out in the implementing act adopted pursuant to this Regulation or the communication form set out in the relevant UNECE regulations referred to in this Regulation or the delegated acts adopted pursuant to this Regulation.

(6) **'System type-approval'** means a type-approval whereby an approval authority certifies that a system built into a vehicle of a specific type satisfies the relevant administrative provisions and technical requirements.

(7) **'Separate technical unit type-approval'** means a type-approval whereby an approval authority certifies that a separate technical unit satisfies the relevant administrative provisions and technical requirements in relation to one or more specified types of vehicles.

(8) **'Component type-approval'** means a type-approval whereby an approval authority certifies that a component independently of a vehicle satisfies the relevant administrative provisions and technical requirements.

(9) **'National type-approval'** means a type-approval procedure laid down by the national law of a Member State, the validity of such approval being restricted to the territory of that Member State.

(10) **'Certificate of conformity'** means the document issued by the manufacturer, which certifies that a produced vehicle conforms to the approved vehicle type.

(11) **'Base vehicle'** means any vehicle which is used at the initial stage of a multi-stage type-approval process.

(12) **'Incomplete vehicle'** means any vehicle which must undergo at least one further stage of completion in order to meet the relevant technical requirements of this Regulation.

(13) **'Completed

L-category vehicles encompass a diverse range of powered two-, three-, and four-wheel vehicles, including powered cycles, mopeds, motorcycles (with or without side-cars), and various types of quads and quadri-mobiles. For regulatory purposes, these vehicles are systematically divided into six primary categories, each with specific subcategories based on design and function. **Category L1e** covers light two-wheel powered vehicles, split into powered cycles (L1e-A) and two-wheel mopeds (L1e-B). **Category L2e** includes three-wheel mopeds, further distinguished between those designed for passenger transport (L2e-P) and utility purposes (L2e-U). **Category L3e** defines two-wheel motorcycles, which are subcategorized by performance levels—low (L3e-A1), medium (L3e-A2), and high (L3e-A3)—as well as special uses such as enduro (E) and trial (T) variants. **Category L4e** specifically refers to two-wheel motorcycles equipped with side-cars. **Category L5e** comprises powered tricycles, divided into passenger-oriented models (L5e-A) and commercial utility tricycles (L5e-B). Finally, **Category L6e** covers light quadricycles, including light on-road quads (L6e-A) and light quadri-mobiles (L6e-B), the latter further split into utility (BU) and passenger (BP) versions, while **Category L7e** handles heavy quadricycles, ranging from heavy on-road quads (L7e-A) and all-terrain quads (L7e-B) to heavy quadri-mobiles (L7e-C) designed for either goods or passenger transport.

Beyond structural classification, these vehicles are also categorized by their propulsion systems. They may be powered by internal combustion engines (compression or positive ignition), external combustion engines or turbines (treated as positive ignition for safety and environmental compliance), pre-compressed air engines, electric motors, or hybrid configurations combining any of these. Additionally, the classification system includes a fallback mechanism: if a vehicle exceeds the criteria for a specific category or subcategory, it is automatically assigned to the next applicable category that it meets, ensuring all vehicles fall within a defined regulatory framework. Finally, while these paragraphs establish the core classification, Annex V may introduce additional subcategories to harmonize international environmental performance testing procedures in alignment with UNECE regulations.

Before a Member State designates a technical service under Article 63, it must verify that the entity satisfies a comprehensive set of nine requirements ensuring independence, competence, and integrity. First, the service must be legally established under national law with distinct legal personality. Crucially, it must operate as a third-party body completely independent from the design, manufacturing, supply, or maintenance of the vehicles, systems, components, or technical units it assesses; while membership in a relevant business association is permissible, the body must demonstrably prove its independence and the absence of conflicts of interest. Furthermore, the service, its top-level management, and the specific personnel responsible for designated activities cannot act as designers, manufacturers, suppliers, or maintainers of the items they assess, nor represent parties engaged in those activities, though the use of assessed units for operational or personal purposes is permitted.

To execute its duties, the technical service must demonstrate to the designating authority that it possesses personnel with appropriate skills, specific technical knowledge, and vocational training, alongside clear, transparent, and reproducible procedures tailored to the complexity of the technology and the scale of production. The service must also have access to all necessary equipment and facilities to perform its tasks in an appropriate manner, while complying with relevant standards set out in delegated acts under Article 65. Operational integrity is paramount: the service and its staff must carry out activities with the highest degree of professional freedom from financial or other pressures that could influence judgment, and they must guarantee impartiality by avoiding any activities that conflict with their independence. Additionally, unless liability is assumed by the Member State, the technical service must maintain liability insurance for its activities. Finally, all personnel are bound by a strict obligation of professional secrecy regarding information obtained during their tasks, with exceptions only for the designating authority or where required by Union or national law, while ensuring the protection of proprietary rights.

By 31 December 2021, Member States were mandated to submit comprehensive reports to the Commission detailing the number of individual approvals granted to L-category vehicles prior to their first registration since 1 January 2016, alongside an analysis of any national criteria that deviated from obligatory EU type-approval requirements. Building upon this data and following a consultation with relevant stakeholders, the Commission was required to finalize its own report by 31 December 2022, addressing these subjects while ensuring alignment with existing European and international standards. This legislative review aimed to evaluate the feasibility of incorporating individual approvals into the Regulation based on harmonised requirements, with the final submission potentially accompanied by legislative proposals to standardize the approval process across the Union.

In accordance with Article 17 of the relevant regulatory framework, the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) is mandated to establish and maintain a centralized, publicly accessible database hosted on the internet. This repository serves as a transparent information hub for investors and market participants, specifically listing all managers of qualifying venture capital funds that have been registered pursuant to Article 14. Beyond identifying the fund managers, the database provides comprehensive details regarding the qualifying venture capital funds they market, including the specific countries in which these funds are offered to investors. By consolidating this data in a single, open-source location, ESMA ensures that stakeholders can easily verify the registration status of fund managers and understand the geographical scope of fund distribution, thereby enhancing market transparency and investor protection across the European Union.

This Regulation shall enter into force on the twentieth day following that of its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union. It shall apply from 22 July 2013, except for Article 9(5), which shall apply from 15 May 2013.

Managers of qualifying venture capital funds are bound by a rigorous code of conduct designed to safeguard investor interests and maintain market integrity. In the execution of their duties, they must **act honestly, fairly, and with due skill, care, and diligence** in all their activities, ensuring that their professional judgment is exercised with the highest standards of competence. To prevent malpractices that could reasonably affect the interests of investors and the portfolio undertakings, managers are required to **apply appropriate policies and procedures** tailored to mitigate specific risks. Their business operations must be conducted in a manner that **promotes the best interests** of the funds, the investors, and the broader market integrity.

Furthermore, managers must exercise a **high level of diligence** throughout the investment lifecycle, from the initial selection of qualifying portfolio undertakings to their ongoing monitoring and support. This commitment to oversight is underpinned by the requirement that managers **possess adequate knowledge and understanding** of the specific companies in which they invest, ensuring they can provide informed guidance. Crucially, they must **treat all investors fairly**, adhering to the principle of equal treatment. Consequently, managers must **ensure that no investor obtains preferential treatment**, unless such an arrangement is explicitly disclosed within the fund's rules or instruments of incorporation, thereby maintaining transparency and trust among all stakeholders.

Managers of qualifying social entrepreneurship funds are required to submit an annual report to the competent authority of their home Member State within six months following the end of each financial year. This comprehensive report must detail the composition of the fund's portfolio and summarize the activities undertaken during the preceding year. Crucially, it must disclose the profits earned by the fund at the time of its liquidation, as well as any profits distributed throughout its operational life, alongside the fund's audited financial accounts. While the report must adhere to existing reporting standards and the specific terms agreed upon between the manager and investors, managers must also provide a copy to investors upon request, with both parties free to agree on additional disclosures.

To ensure transparency regarding the fund's social mission, the annual report must explicitly include: (a) details of the overall social outcomes achieved by the investment policy and the methodology used to measure them; (b) a statement of any divestments made from qualifying portfolio undertakings; (c) a description of whether divestments from non-qualifying assets occurred based on specific criteria outlined in Article 14(1)(f); (d) a summary of activities the manager undertook in relation to qualifying portfolio undertakings as defined in Article 14(1)(l); and (e) information regarding the nature and purpose of any investments that do not qualify under Article 5(1). Furthermore, an independent audit must be conducted at least annually to confirm that all money and assets are held in the fund's name and that the manager maintains adequate records and controls over the use of these assets and the investors' mandates. Finally, if the manager is already required to publish an annual financial report under Directive 2004/109/EC, the information specified in the paragraphs above may be submitted either as a separate document or as an additional section of that existing financial report.

In accordance with the regulatory framework governing social entrepreneurship, the Commission is mandated to conduct a comprehensive review of this Regulation to assess the effectiveness and evolution of the rules established therein. This evaluation will encompass a broad survey of the practical application of the designation 'EuSEF' across various Member States, examining both domestic and cross-border utilization by fund managers. The review will further analyze the geographical and sectoral distribution of investments made by qualifying funds, while critically assessing the sufficiency of current information requirements under Article 14 to ensure investors can make fully informed decisions.

Furthermore, the Commission will investigate the impact of different qualifying investments on the development of social undertakings throughout the Union and evaluate the potential necessity of establishing a European label for 'social enterprises.' A specific focus will be placed on the feasibility of allowing third-country social entrepreneurship funds to adopt the 'EuSEF' designation, considering existing experiences with international tax governance standards. The review will also scrutinize the practical application of criteria for identifying qualifying portfolio undertakings, the procedures used to measure positive social impact, and the possibility of introducing harmonized Union-level standards for such measurements. Additionally, it will explore the extension of marketing rights to retail investors, the inclusion of these funds within eligible assets under Directive 2009/65/EC, the need for a depositary regime, and the existence of tax obstacles or incentives. Finally, the assessment will identify barriers impeding investment in 'EuSEF' funds, including the influence of prudential Union law on institutional investors.

This review is scheduled to be conducted with specific timelines: points (a) through (e) and (g) through (m) are to be completed by 22 July 2017, while point (f) is to be addressed by 22 July 2015. Following this analysis and after consulting ESMA, the Commission shall submit a report to the European Parliament and the Council, which may be accompanied by a legislative proposal if deemed appropriate.

By 15 March 2015, and biennially thereafter, Member States are mandated to submit comprehensive reports to the Commission detailing their national frameworks for tracking policies and measures, alongside projections of anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions and removals. These submissions must include updates to their reporting systems if previously described, progress on low-carbon development strategies, and a sectoral breakdown of national and Union measures organized by gas type (specifically HFCs and PFCs). Each reported measure must specify its objectives, the policy instrument used, implementation status, monitoring indicators, and quantitative estimates of emission effects. Crucially, these estimates must distinguish between emissions covered by Directive 2003/87/EC and Decision No 406/2009/EC, providing both ex ante assessments for a four-year future sequence and ex post evaluations where available. The reports should also cover projected and realized cost-benefit analyses, references to underlying technical reports, and an analysis of how domestic actions complement international mechanisms like Joint Implementation, the CDM, and emissions trading. Furthermore, Member States must notify the Commission of any substantial changes to this data within the first year of the reporting period and ensure that all relevant cost-effectiveness assessments, implementation data, and methodological details are made publicly available in electronic format.

Under the established framework for climate governance, the Commission shall be assisted by a dedicated Climate Change Committee, which functions as a formal committee within the scope of Regulation (EU) No 182/2011. This regulatory structure ensures that the Committee operates under the standardized rules governing the exercise of implementing powers by the Commission. Consequently, whenever a reference is made to this specific provision, Article 5 of Regulation (EU) No 182/2011 shall apply, thereby defining the precise procedural mechanisms for the Committee's role in the decision-making process.
This Regulation shall enter into force on the twentieth day following that of its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union.

For the purposes of this Regulation, a comprehensive set of definitions establishes the framework for measuring, reporting, and managing greenhouse gas activities. **Global warming potential (GWP)** quantifies the total contribution to global warming from one unit of a specific gas relative to carbon dioxide (CO₂), which serves as the reference gas with a value of 1. To track these emissions, a **national inventory system** is defined as the institutional, legal, and procedural framework within a Member State used to estimate anthropogenic emissions and removals of greenhouse gases not controlled by the Montreal Protocol, ensuring data is reported and archived in line with UNFCCC and Kyoto Protocol decisions. The entities responsible for compiling this data are the **competent inventory authorities**, while **quality assurance (QA)** refers to the planned review procedures designed to meet data quality objectives and support the effectiveness of the overall program. Complementing this, **quality control (QC)** encompasses routine technical activities aimed at ensuring data integrity, correctness, and completeness by identifying errors, documenting materials, and recording all QA activities.

The regulation further defines key metrics for progress and trading mechanisms. An **indicator** is any quantitative or qualitative factor that helps understand policy implementation and emission trends. Specific trading units include the **assigned amount unit (AAU)**, **removal unit (RMU)**, and **emission reduction unit (ERU)**, all issued pursuant to Decision 13/CMP.1. Under Article 12 of the Kyoto Protocol, various credit types are recognized: the **certified emission reduction (CER)**, the **temporary certified emission reduction (tCER)** for afforestation projects replaceable at the end of the second commitment period, and the **long-term certified emission reduction (lCER)** for long-term removals replaceable upon project expiry or storage reversal. All these units, along with others, are recorded in a **national registry**, a standardized electronic database tracking their issue, holding, transfer, cancellation, and other lifecycle events.

The regulation also clarifies the scope of action and evaluation. **Policies and measures** encompass all instruments aiming to implement UNFCCC commitments, even if emission reduction is not their primary objective. These are managed through a **system for policies and measures and projections**, which reports on both **ex ante assessments** (projected effects) and **ex post assessments** (past effects) of such policies. Projections are categorized into three types: **projections without measures** (excluding future policies), **projections with measures** (including adopted

By January 15 of each year (designated as year X), Member States are legally obligated to submit comprehensive greenhouse gas inventories to the European Commission, covering data from the preceding two years (year X-2) and, where applicable, the prior three years (year X-3). This reporting cycle requires a detailed breakdown of anthropogenic emissions for gases listed in Annex I, alongside specific pollutants such as carbon monoxide, sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and volatile organic compounds, all aligned with UNFCCC standards. A critical provision within this framework stipulates that for the purposes of specific EU decisions, CO₂ emissions from civil aviation (IPCC category 1.A.3.A) shall be treated as zero. The submission must also include a granular analysis of Land Use, Land-Use Change, and Forestry (LULUCF) activities, detailing emissions and removals by sources and sinks, with additional reporting required for specific activities like cropland management and wetland drainage if they are accounted for. Member States must justify any revisions to previously reported data and provide indicators, registry information regarding the trading of allowances (AAUs, CERs, etc.), and summaries of international cooperation mechanisms like Joint Implementation or the Clean Development Mechanism. Furthermore, the reports must demonstrate the quality and consistency of the data by including uncertainty assessments, descriptions of national inventory system changes, and cross-checks against verified emissions from the EU Emissions Trading System and air pollutant directives. While Member States must provide preliminary data by January 15 and final LULUCF data by March 15 of the second year following the accounting period, the complete national inventory report containing all listed information is due to the Commission by March 15 of each year. Following this, Member States must forward their national inventories to the UNFCCC Secretariat by April 15, enabling the Commission to compile and submit the consolidated Union greenhouse gas inventory report to the UNFCCC by the same April 15 deadline.

Confidentiality and data protection form the bedrock of the Office's investigative framework, ensuring that all information transmitted or obtained—whether during external or internal inquiries—is rigorously safeguarded. Information gathered in the course of external investigations is protected under relevant provisions, while data arising from internal investigations is strictly subject to professional secrecy and the specific protections afforded to Union institutions. The institutions, bodies, offices, and agencies involved share a collective responsibility to ensure the confidentiality of these investigations is maintained, balancing this duty with the legitimate rights of the persons concerned and adhering to all applicable national rules where judicial proceedings are initiated. To further strengthen this framework, the Office may designate a Data Protection Officer in accordance with Article 24 of Regulation (EC) No 45/2001. Furthermore, the Director-General is tasked with ensuring that any information released to the public is presented neutrally and impartially, strictly respecting investigation confidentiality and complying with the principles outlined in this Article and Article 9(1). Finally, in line with the Staff Regulations, all Office staff are bound by an absolute obligation to refrain from unauthorized disclosure of information received in the line of duty, unless such information is already public or accessible to the public; this duty of secrecy persists even after their service has ended.

The Supervisory Committee serves as a critical oversight mechanism designed to reinforce the independence of the Office in exercising its investigative competences. Composed of five independent members with senior judicial or investigative experience, appointed by common accord of the European Parliament, the Council, and the Commission, the Committee operates with a strict mandate to avoid seeking or taking instructions from any government or institution. Its primary function is to regularly monitor the implementation of the Office's investigative duties, specifically focusing on procedural guarantees and the duration of investigations based on information supplied by the Director-General.

In carrying out this monitoring role, the Committee addresses opinions and recommendations to the Director-General regarding necessary resources, investigative priorities, and investigation timelines. These opinions can be initiated by the Committee itself, requested by the Director-General, or prompted by other EU institutions, provided they do not interfere with ongoing investigations. Furthermore, in duly justified situations, the Committee may request additional information or reports on closed investigations. The Committee is also empowered to appoint its own chair, adopt its own rules of procedure (subject to prior information from key EU bodies), and hold at least ten meetings annually, with decisions made by a majority vote.

Regarding tenure, members serve non-renewable five-year terms, with staggered replacements to preserve institutional expertise; upon the expiry of their term, they remain in office until a successor is appointed. Members receive daily allowances and expense reimbursements in accordance with Commission rules. If a member ceases to meet the required conditions or is found guilty of serious misconduct, they may be relieved of their duties by the same appointing bodies acting in common accord. Finally, the Committee ensures transparency by adopting an annual report assessing the Office's independence and procedural application, which is sent to the European Parliament, the Council, the Commission, and the Court of Auditors, while also having the discretion to submit specific reports on investigation results and subsequent actions.

**18 Financing**

The total appropriations allocated to the Office, which explicitly encompass the funding required for the Supervisory Committee and its secretariat, shall be recorded under a designated budget line within the section of the general budget of the European Union pertaining to the Commission. To ensure transparency and clarity in resource allocation, these financial provisions shall be elaborated in detail within an Annex specifically attached to that budget section.
